div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

"Turn men and they will trust you," said Emerson. "Trust men and they will bust you," says the average business man. "TEE pleasantest way to take cod-liver oil," , says an old gourmand, "is to fatten pigeons with it, and then eat the pigeons." A PERMANENT ATTRACTION.—CIara : "Are you not afraid that some one will marry you for your money?' Dora: " I would rather be married for money than for beauty." "Of all things! Why ?" "Beauty fades, but money can be kept at interest." LASTED A LONG TlME.—Willis : "When my wife makes me a present it is sure to be something that will last." Wallace: "My wife is just like her. Five years ago she made me a present of a hundred cigars, and I have ninety-nine of them yet." MEN never take their wives fishing with them if they can help it. There are so few women who will go fishing with their husbands, and agree to everything the husbands tell when they come back. SHE WAS TIP.ED.—" Well, may I hope, then, dearest, that at some time I may have the happi- ness of making you my wife?' "Yes, I hope so, I am sure," she replied. "I am tired of suing fellows for breach of promise." DISSIPATION.—" I don't know what I'm going to do about my husband," said the owl, with a sob. "What's the matter ?" asked the sympathetic nightingale. "His habits are getting to be some- what dreadful. This is the second time this week that he has been up all day.' DIFFICULT, BUT SATISFACTORY. Mamma: "What are you trying to draw ?" Little Ethel : "A elephant." "Rather a difficult subject." "I'd rather draw elephants than anything else, because my friends can always tell what it is. They knows a elephant is the only animal wif two tails." "PAPA," said Willie, "I wish you'd tell me. If you were Queen Victoria and mamma was the Emperor of China--- Got that ?" " Yes." " Well, if you was they, who I'd be ?" MARRIED MAN "Why don't you get married, Miss Perkins? You are getting to look like a back number '—you will soon be an 01l maid." Miss Perkins: "If I were as easy to please as your wife was, I would have been married long ago." MOTHER: "When do you suppose that young man who calls upon you will make known his in- tentions, Laura ?' Laura: "I think he will pro- pose pretty soon. Last evening he was very anxious to know whether I could dress on £2O a year." PRETTY WIFE: "I knew you'd like this new hat, darling. It is becoming, and nothing could be simpler, could it?" Darling (thoughtfully) : "Nothing, except the man who has to pay three guineas for it." GROWING YOUNG AGAIN.—Two ladies discovered talking in a corner of the drawing-room: "Had not Mrs. M— grey hair last year ? " "Yea" "How does it happen to be black now?" You forget, my dear, that she has lost her husband since then." AUNT: "I want to do something to please you on your birthday, Charlie ; but first I want to ask your teacher how you behave in school." Charlie : "If you really wish to please me, auntie, don't as him." PEOPLE who wonder why men's hair turns grey before their whiskers should remember that there is about twenty years' differenoe in their respective

ages. WHEN WE FEEL SMALL.—"There are times," &aid the man with the oratorical manner, "when we are overwhelmed with humiliation at the powerlessness of the human mind." "That's very true," was the reply. " I am often made to feel so." " Indeed ?' "Yes. I have a four-year-old daughter who asks questions." CRUELTY TO AN INFANT.—" Plow did it happen that Bidgs was arrested by an agent for the Society for the I'revention of Cruelty to Children ?" "He was caught in the act of abusing his baby." "What was he doing?" "Singing it to sleep." "I SAW your name in print the other day," said one man to another, who was very fond of notoriety. "Where ?" asked the other, in pleased excitement. " In the directory ' LOVING MOTHER: "I cannot understand what makes our boy, Robert, so fond of pedestrianism." Fond Father; "He gets that from me. Didn't I walk the floor with him for weeks when he was a baby." " THREE kinds of juries figure prominently in trials now," remarked McCorckle. "What are they ?" asked McCrackle. "Grand jury, common jury, and perjury." BOTH SATISFIED.—EsteIIa : "What a lovely ball! I never enjoyed myself so much in all my life." Gladys: "Nor I." E•aella : "I danced every dance, and had a different partner each time." Gladys: "I sat out every dance, and had the same partner all the evening !" Miss ANTIQUE (school teacher) : "What does w-h-i-t-e sell?' Class—no answer. Miss An. : "What is the colour of my skin?' Class (in chorus) : " Y how." "Paw people," said the wife, as she proceeded to investigate her husband's pockets after he had gone to sleep—" few people are aware of what a wife has to go through. ' A SPOILED PUBLIC.—Boy: "Paper, sir ?" Up- todate "Well, I don't know. Have you any paper that prints coupons which you can take to the office next day and exchange for a fresh paper ?" GOLDRICH : "I've fixed it so that there will be no contest over my will." Silvercash : " Impos- sible." Goldrich "Not at aIL I've left every- thing to the lawyers." A LABOuR PESSIMIST.—Agitator : "Oi've been all over this town, and it's goin' to the dogs; that's phwat it is." Mechanic: "What's wrong with it ?" Agitator: "Oi can't get up a stroike any- where." SPOKE FROM EXPERIENCE. —Temperance Orator: "Even an innocent baby has a wonderful influence over a man." Man on Back Seat: " Righ you are, stranger. That's what drove me to drink.' NEVER bear morg than one kind of trouble at a time. Some people bear three kinds—ad they have had, all they have now, and all they expect to have. A FARMER sW a recipe advertised for keeping wells and cincrus from freezing in winter. Having sent a dozen stamps he received the following: "Take in your well or cistern at night, and stand it in front of the fire.' A "LORD OF REATION."—A hen-pecked hus- band called the servant maid aside, and said: "Look here, Rebustina, I am told that my wife and daughtee-. are planning a trip to Biarritz ; do you know whether I am going w,th them or not?" APARTMENTS TO LET.—We cull the following advertisement from a German paper; "Furnished apartments for a gentleman 12 feet long and 10 feet wide. PRISCILLA : "They say that Clara's hair is not her own." Prunella : "Do they? What a shame! W;v, she showed me a receipted bill for it the other day." " Was your watchman well recommended ?" "Oh, not directly. I used to see him in church, and as lie stayed awake all through Dr. Sono-a's sermons, I concluded he was the man I. wanted," " YES, sir," said Jenkins; "Smithers is a man who keeps his word; but then he has to." "How is that?' asked Johnson. "Because no one will take it." _ SHOPPING IN THE COUNTRY.—" NO, ma'am ; those are two articles we don't kee ; but the oysters, I think, you will find at the post-office, and the onions you can get aaross the way, at the barber's.' " how are you finain, business' doctor ?" was asked of a physician. "'Capital,' he replied; "I have all I can attend to." "I didn't understand that, there was much id,,ess about." "No, there isn't. But we pny,i.A.ns do not depend upon siesiness for an inco e. On, no; most of our money is made from people who have nothing the matter with theta." V, HAT HE REMEMBEILED.—Bright Boy "Uncle •George took me to hear a lecture on phrenology." Father: "Let me see if yeu can tell me what you lee rued ?' Bright Boy: Some smart men have high foreheads, and some smart men have low foreheads; and some big fool, nave high forehea and some Mg fools have low foreheads. That s all I can remember." • Dip you give sister the larger part of the as I told you?' "Yes, mamma." "TbS4 is noble. And did you not feel happier for it! Yeim. Her part was rotten."

div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

Lord Selborne's action in taking his seat in the House of Commons on Monday night has given rise to extreme dissatisfaction among the Conservative rank and tile. As usual, Mr. Chamberlain is blamed for the new sensation, although I am told that pri- vately Lord Selborne takes the whole responsibility on his own shoulders. There is good ground for belier ing that he had not settled on the course ef action which he has now adopted even so late as on Friday night, and strong influence was brought to bear to induce him to let the matter rest. I rather fancy that but for Mr. George Curzon's re- turn from America he might have yielded to this pressure. But Mr.Curzon is nothing if not enter- prising ; and, backed by his sympathy and that of Brodrick, Lord Selborne was advised to take the step which has given rise to so much excite- ment in Parliamentary circles. Mr. Chamberlain was certainly not formally committed, but I think there can be no doubt that the members directly concerned in the matter were pretty confident that they would not be without his sympathy. The disgust of the Conservatives generally is, however, unconcealed. They think that this revolt against the responsibilites of the peerage on the part of the Conservative and Liberal Unionist members of Parliament is bound to prejudice the Upper House very hardly in the eyes of the constituencies in the struggle which is impending. I may say, by the way, that the member of Parliament to whom Mr. Chamberlain referred as being the heir to a peerage which he has never claimed is generally understood to be Sir James Carmichael, one of the members for Glasgow, who is supposed to be an English peer in his own right.

The " Daily News "Naples correspondent writes: —" I saw De Lucia [a e great tenor] previc,ns te his departure for London. He said he always goes to London as if to a country holiday, where, in spite of his operatic work, he really rests, enjoying the parks and lovely surroundings of the vast city. He is fond of the London audiences—so serious, quiet, and polite, yet at the same time sympathe- tic and appreciative. London, in tact, has become the darling of his heart, the city in which he best likes to sing."

I learn that, in spite of the somewhat unsatisfac- tory, or at least contradictory reports respecting the state of affairs at the New Australia colony in Paraguay, a British Board has been formed for the benefit of would-be colonists in this country. The Board, which consists of -those members who intend to emigrate and others, is represented by a small committee havinFi the power to accept new mem- bers, grant interimcertificates of association,arrange for the passage of the sanguine, and generally to carry on propagandist work. The seceders from the original New Australia Co-operative Settlement, numbering about fifty men, women, and children, are known as the Cosme Colony, and it is reported that they are plar.ting bananas, orange trees, peach trees, and vines, as well as cultivating grain and vegetables, and that ttey work eight hours a day five days a week. It would be interesting to know how the colonists "put in" the rest of their time.

The annual meeting of the Fabian Society, which has just been held, disclosed a rift in the lute; but it was not of a very serious character, ani was healed up in a sensible manner. A vote of censure was to have been moved by.one of the more un- compromising members of the society against Mr. Sydney Webb and two or three other members at the organisation, for having stood at various recent elections in London as Progressi 7e candidates, against rival candidates run by the Social Democra- tic Federation and the Independent Labour party. All three are Socialist bodies. The competition of the Socialist candidates therefore becomes curious. The gentleman who intended to bring the motion forward had thrown himself into the Wal worth election, with the view of promoting the cause of the Socialist candidate, and did not present himself to lead his charge against Mt. Webb. The subject was debated, nevertheless, under the guise of a new motion from the opposite side, which was carried by an overwhelming majority, that the society de- clined, according to its established practice, to in- terfere with the political conduct of its members. It is interesting to observe that some .very severe oriticism was levelled at the Independent Labour party for its policy ot extreme isolation from Pro- gressive Liberalism. This came naturally from a horly like the Fabians, who are above all things Opportuniste,and who • object is to seize every occa- Nion and every instrument for the furtherance of ocialism.
The month of June will witness the most remark, able women's demonstration in London of renew

times. There is to be a woman's campaign on a gigantic scale. On one Sunday, in the middle of the month, no fewer than 200 pulpits will be occu- pied by women. These lady preachers will deliver special sermons, harangues, or discourses on religion. on Temperance, and on morals, according to the idiosyncracy of the fair enthusiast. The pulpits have all been secured, 80 that there is no danger of the demonstration breaking down. An irruption of the fair sex into a religious and social propaganda on a scale of this kind,is something novel in history and is an indication of what is coming. Even Fashion and Frivolity and the New Woman may tremble.

There is a great deal of well-funded dissatis- faction in naval circles at the niggardliness of the Government in throwing upon the officers who are to take part in the ceremonial opening of the Baltic Canal the cost of entertainment. Ihe admirals enjoy a happy exemption from this burden, as they receive a SUM for table allowance ; but the ordin- ury naval officers have no such privilege. It seems a mean ploceeding to ship men off to an inter- national ceremony, and to leave them to meet out of their private funds the expense of the courtesies which the ceremony involves. I believe in foreign navies the necessary outlay is refunded. On the occasion of the visit of the French fleet to Ports- mouth recently, an allowance was made to the English officers, and the Admiralty or the 1 reasury would not lose in popularity if this precedent were followed on the present occasion.

The tour of the Ameer's son during b 8 residence in this country will be very ex ensive, though he cannot be lionised as his lather would have been. He will be taken to all the centres of inserestin the provinces, and he will, of course, visit Liverpool among other places. The shipping of the great port on the Mersey will probably impress him even more than that of the Thames. It is expected that he will be more attached by the industrial and mechanical wonders of the Black Country, and some kindred places, than be will even be in the display of our mercantile marine, as he may be supposed to be interested in his father's workshops in Cabal.. Our deckyards will of course be visited, and there will be sight-seeing at Elswick, in addition to what can be seen at Woolwich or Portsmouth, at Sheffield, Leeds, Newcastle, the Lancashire spinning towns, I and Edinburgh and Glasgow.

A very satisfactory collection. of historical and ' antique clocks and watches was opened on Wednes- day at the Aquarium. Over 1,700 in number, the exhibits are arranged in one of the long galleries. The greater number of the watches are lent by Mr. Evan Roberts, Southport. These include watches which once belonged to Lady Jane Grey, Queen Elizabeth, Calvin, James 1., Milton, Bunyan, New- ton, William 111,, George 111., and Robert Burns. Among the clocks is a Sabbatarian timekeeper, con- 4ructed by a Scotchman in the last century, which wa. made to stop at midnight on Saturday until the same hour on Sunday, on which day the dial is t,idclen by a lettered monition to "remember the Sal hath." This, however, is only one among many . .

plendid specimens of a craft which there is too much reasois to believe is, as far as England is con- cerned. a decaying industry. Yet there are in this exhibition proofs that the craft need not be alto- gether handed over to German and American work- men if only makers will adopt modern methods.

Buttermilk. Among the many evidences of extravagance in wast- ing our food resources, there are few more striking th.n the waste of milk. Anyone who has lived in Lancashire, or travelled in Scotland or Ireland, and has noted th. life and characteristic food of the farmers and of th, peasantry, will know how pleasant and acceptable a drink of buttermilk is. On the first day it is a thin iini semi-acidulous beverge, refreshing and full of iviorisl- ment; on the second day thicker and richer, and more nearly resembling the familiar curds and whey,but with a curd broken into fine particles, and therefore les, cloyins and more digestible. The waste of buttermilk is very, great.and yet half a pint contains as much Tintrl. ment, and is as sustaining a beverage, as many gallons of beer.

The Fashionable Colour in Hair. The newest colour for hair is a deep yellow, alm .st verging on red, writes a contemporary. Last season a ruddy tinge was indispensable to the woman of fashion. but to-day waved tresses of vs l ant brass or copper cohsur are coiled behind the head of the mondaine. With a , change of hair tint a change of complPxion is in.lispens- able, and lithe new hue is much adopted the rouge and powder must needs be altered to correspond. If this is to he a season of make-up—a consummation devoutly not to be wished—it is to be hoped that the blue or purple-complexioned woman will not be sPen in our mid 4. Some kinds of powder have this horrible eff,e.f, hich is presumably unknown to the lady herself, for whn 'would elect to don a violet complexion even to match a violet gown ? Last season thPre was a notab'e absence of make-up among girls a pleasing contrast to the season of a few years ago, ;hen sweet nineteen a.cl twenty spoilt their round cheeks with rouge, and did ~p their eyebrows. It was not a season of many marriages, hence, perhaps, the reaction in favour of natural com- plexions.

You be .. with the frilled blouses. White cambric models have white frills, or frills edged with a band of pink or blue. The pretty, plain, hem-stitched frilling is much used for the purpose. These frills edge the pleat down the centre of the front. They edge the broad turn-over collar and the tight cuffs of the voluminous bishop's sleeves. A dressy blouse of silk-figured crepon is arranged in deep blouse pleats—two on the right and two on the left of a lace plastron, which is finished with a fluted lace bow at the neck. Smart blouses are made of shot and chine silks in dainty colourings. Some of the dressy blouses have draped collars of the blouse material, decorated with a lace butterfly bow, but even more than the sailor collar—which at present seems to promise an overwhelming omnipresence—made of linen edged with a frill of cambric or lace, or made entirely of lace. Blouses should be worn pulling well over the waistbelt—that is, they should not be drawn down too tightly beneath the skirt. The waistbelt should be wide and handsome. Black satin ribbon is the favourite material. Some very pretty after- noon blouses are made of crepon with draped belt forming a slight point back and front. These French blouses have boned linings, which are as closely fitted as a bodice, the blouse effect being obtained by draping the material on the lining. The English cotton blouses mostly partake of the " shirt " character, and are characterised by simplicity. Among the neatest blouses I have seen was one made of spotted fawn surah silk and shot rose. It had large full sleeves. The yoke was trimmed with two bands of tiny gathers, which almost re- sembled a necklet, and the collar band was frilled at the sides, fastening at the back. There was a delightful little bow at the waist.

In regard to millinery, the flowers selected seem o be larger than ever—monstrous chrysanthemums, shaded hydrangeas, giant orchids, phenomenal poppies, roses of immense size and most glowing colours. Lace is plentifully used, and is daily ex- tending into monstrous fans and gigantic butter- flies all covered with spangles. The ribbons used are becoming wider and wider, forming scarves, great loops, enormous rosettes. It is possible to speak in favour of the pretty supple straws, in beautiful shades like Nice rose, sky blue, pale green, cream white, as well as in all the usual darker shades like bronze, red, navy. The texture of the straw has borrowed something from the crepons, and each is gauffred and waved in charm- ing fashion. In marked contrast with the gigantic hats used for dressy wear, are the graceful little capotes, all jetted or embroidered with gold or silver, simply trimmed with bouquets. These are in excellent style, which the majority of large hats are not. The picture hats op of different sizes. The brim of a pretty model is made of net,
the lace edge being outlined in fancy straw. The crown should be high, and be trinuned with chiffon, roses, osprey and shot ribbon. This is a very stylish hat.
Your loving JENNIE.

div.head: PARTED AT THE ALTAR;
div.p: PARTED AT THE ALTAR;
BY LAURA JEAN LIBREY,
Author of "A Mad Betrothal," "lone," "Parted by Fate," " Floribel s Lover," etc., etc.

CHAPTER XXVII. DORIS AND FREDERICK MEET AGAIN. FOR three long and weary years Frederick Thornton travelled incessantly; but his great effort to forget Doris was all in vain. The sweet, dimpled, gi fish face was between him and the suustiine—filled his thoughts—made his life one long regret. " How strange it was," be often told himself, "that he had discovered his love for poor, pretty Doris in the very hour that he had lost her so cruelly !" Three years had made little change in Frederick Thorn on. He was the same handsome Frederick as of old; all save the gay, laughing sparkle in the dark, expressive eyes. That had died out of them for ever, leaving them thoughtful and gloomy, wi h a look of brooding melancholy in them that never left them. Pretty young gir s sighed and smiled at the handsome American all in vain. He seemed to be oblivious to the charms of fair women, or else marble-hearted they often declared. After three years of incessant travelling, fate brought him, one sunlit June morning, to a little village in Kent, lying among the hills. He was delighted to dud there was a party of Ameri.ans stopping at the villa across the way. Strolling out upon the pizza of the hostelry, the first person whom his eyes rested upon was his old college hum, Karl Lancaster. " Well, by all that's wonderful, if it isn't Fred Thornton !" exclaimed Karl, chee ily, a he wrung his old friend's hand in the rea,test delight. "This is, indeed, a surprise. Where in the world did you drop from ?" " ame up from London for a few weeks' quiet," exclaimed Frederick, adding : I return to New York at he end of the month." " The deuce you do !" exclaimed Karl, impul- sively. "Do you think I shall consent to lose my old chum so easily? No. indeed ! You will make a valuable acquisition to our little party." "Who is there among your party ?" inquired Frederick. "Only my mother and fa, her, father's ward— Miss Fielding—and myself. We have just got rid of two noble lords and an earl who persisted in following us about from place to place, having been smitten with father's ward ; finding their suit useless, one by one gave up in despl.ir, and went his way." Frederic smiled. "You must come over and dine with us to-day, and 1 wili preseut you to Miss Fielding; but I warn you beforehand, do not attempt to fall in love with her." "No doub you have hopes in that direction," smiled Thu nton. "But you need not fear a rival be me. I have gotten over being a beauty worshipper. I always avoid women, when I oath" " I hope you are not going to turn out a cynical woman-hater," declared Karl. "That would never do. Never!' " I shall expect you to dine with us to-day, and I shall not take •No for an answer,' said Karl again. at ear "In that case, it would be useless to give any other answer than one in the affirmative,' smiled Frederick; "so I shall probably put in an appear- ance some time during the afternoon. Kindly remember me to your father and mother.' After a little the friends parted, Karl going to- ward the villa, and Frederick Thornton strolling leisurely down the flower-strewn path that led toward the river that lay smiling beyond. How long he stood there, in a dreamy reverie, on the primrose-bordered bank he never knew. He was aroused at length by the sound of hurried footsteps, and turning his head slightly, a sight met his view that he never forgot until his dying doy. From an abrupt curve in the path—seemingly from out of the very heart of a thicket of roses—stepped a yo. ng girl, a tall, slim, lovely creature, graceful as a fawu, with a face so radiantly lovely in its fair, dimpled, girlish beauty as to almost take his breath away at the first fatal glance. Surely the summer sunlight had never fallen upon a fairer picture than this beautiful, golden-haired young girl. She was hurry ng along so swiftly, she did not percei‘e the tall, handsome stranger leaning ag .inst the trunk of a tree, gazing at her so intently. She passed so near Frederick, he could have put out his hand and touched her dress; and suddenly, in that instant, a passmg sportive breeze caught the broad sun-hat that was tilted down over her curls, lifted it from her head, and hurled it directiy at Frederick Thornton's feet. Quickly he stooped to recover it. "Permit me," he said, extending the hat by its blue ribbons with one hand, and raising his own with a cour eons bow with the other. The youeg eh I started back with a low cry of terror, and er, ked into his face, clutching one hand tightly over hei heart. As the reader has already imagined, it was Doris. A ter three long years she stood face to face with Frederick Thornton again. And she saw, too, that be did not recognise her, so great was the change in her. Ah, it was little wonder he did not, believing Doris to be lying cold in her grave on the other side of the Atlantic. He heard the low, gasping cry, and saw the blanching of the lovely dimpled cheeks. "I beg a thousand pardons if I have startled you," he said, eagerly. "I fancied you must have _seen me standing here as you came down the

path." Doris received the hat from his hand with a little nervous bow. She could not trust herself to answe- him, so great was her emotion. What reply she made, she never knew. Turning away, she hurried swiftly °own the path. "Frederick Thornton !" she murmured, pant- ingly, when she was quite out of sight and hearing—" Ah, Heaven, what can he be doing here ?" She was so strangely excited, flushing and paling by turns, that she quite alarmed Mrs. Lancaster when she returned to the villa. • "Why, what is the matter, my dear Doris ?" she exclaimed, in dismay. "Really, you look as though you had seen a ghost." Before Doris could reply she went on quickly: "I want you to look your best this evening, Doris dear, for Karl brings an old friend to dine with us—a Mr. Thornton. He was a great friend of Karl's at College. I have known his family intimately for years.' "You will have to excuse me this evening, Mrs. Lancaster," pleaded Doris. "I have the most severe headache I have over had in all my life." Looking into the flushed face and unnaturally brilliant eyes, who could doubt it? "Lie down and take a rest, my dear," sug- gested Mrs. Lancaster. "You will be all right by evening." Still Doris lingered. How she longed to ask if Vivian was with him, but pride forbade. Of course, believing himself free, he had married Vivian long since. Frederick Thornton had stood gazing after that slim, girlish figure with the strangest sensation at his heart that he had ever experienced. "Pshaw I" he muttered, impatiently, striking a match, and proceeding to light a cigar. " Some- how the features of that young girl's face remind me strangely of poor little Doris. Perhaps Doris would have grown into just such a superb creature, if she had lived. Can that be Miss Fielding, I wonder ?" he mused. During the remainder of the morning Frede-ick Thornton caught himself thinking contmually of the young girl he had met in the glen. He presented himself punctually at the villa. The doctor and his good wife, and Karl, welcomed him cordially; but the face he longed to see (if, indeed, the pretty young girl he had met was Miss Fielding) was not there. "I am sorry Miss Fielding has a headache, and cannot be presented to you,' said said Mrs. Lancaster, "However, this is not to be your last visit to the villa; we shall expect to see a great deal of you while you are staying in the village." "Perhaps I have met Miss Fielding already," replied Frederick, smiling; and he proceeded to recount the adventure of the morning, minutely describing the young girl. "Yes, that is my husband's ward," declared Mrs. Lancaster. "How shrewd you are at gues- sing, my dear Mr. Thornton." From that day Frederick Thornton found an opportunity to call every day at the villa, but by some strange chance he was never able to find the doctor's lovely young ward there. Once he fancied he saw the flutter of a white dress leaving the library by one door as he entered by another. At last he surprised her one chy by entering,. quite unobserved, with Mrs. Lancaster, an hour earlier than he usually called. For a single instant • the room seemed whirling around Doris. As in a dream_ ska heard Ms& Lancaster go through the

formula of the introduction. She heard Frederick Thornton say, "I am happy to meet you, Miss Fielding," then to her dismay, Mrs. Lancaster was called away, and they were left alone together. He had looked into her eyes, heard her voice, and had not recognised her; and she told herself, xvith a bitter smile, that she would never betray her identity to him--never! He should never know that ' she was the same Doris to whom he had been bound by tha,, fatal midnight marriage, and who had de- serted her so cruelly at the altar almost. He had not grieved to have the fetters that bound him to her- self snapped asunder by her death, she felt sure. 0 t course, he was Vivian's husband long since, and could, therefore, be nothing to her now—less than nothing—and quite unconsciously her face grew cold, hard and haughty with superb scorn as he gazed at her. At that moment Karl entered the drawing-room, and Doris took the opportunity to escape from his presence, instantly. Frederick Thornton looked after Miss Fielding in wonder not unmixed with pique. Why did this lovely young girl take such an aversion to him at first sight? Why did she avoid him so persistently? he asked himself, vexedly. He could not under- stand, yet, despite this knowledge, he seemed drawn as by a magnet each day to the villa.

CHAPTER XXVIII. A SHADOW. THAT one glance at the dark, handsome face ot Frederick Thornton awakened all the old bitter- sweet memories in Doris's heart again. She tried to avoid him, but for an hour Frederick Thornton followed Doris about like a shadow. One evening they met at a grand ball. Doris had heard them say he would not be there. Therefore she was much surprised to see him standing by her side. "Are you engaged for the next waltz, Miss Fielding?' he asked, taking the programme from her hand. Doris drew back, her lovely face paling. Even her lips lost their colour. Waltz with him I Ah, no! She could not. How could she feel his breath upon her cheek, the clasp of his strong arm around her, and know that he was another's—that he had lost her for ever-more? "I should prefer dancing any other than a waltz with you, Mr. Thornton,' she said. He certainly felt pique 1. Any other young lady in that grand, glittering ball room would have been pleased to have waltzed with him, he wel• knew. "May I put my name down for the nest quadrille, then ?" he asked, with charming grace; and as Doris could find no reasonable excuse for refusing him, she bowed a cold assent. To her horror, she found it was, after all, a waltz quadrille. She could not escape from him when they were out on the floor together. She vs' obliged to go through the dance with him. Yet Frederick Thornton could not help but notice how she shrank from the touch of his hand and the clasp of his arm. And again he asked himself in the deepest won- der, why had this young girl taken such an aversion to him.

That one waltz-quadrille undid the work of years. Doris had thought that she had steeled her heart against him; but love was not to be disciplined thus easily. She realised that Doris of twenty loved handsome Frederick Thornton a thousand times more deeply than the Doris of seventeen had done. That was childish, beautiful love; this was the full, passionate strength of a woman's love—the love that blesses or curses human hear, s. _ _

From that hour Frederick Thornton followed Doris about like a shadow. He took great care to place himself in every set with her, If she strolled out on the balcony, on looking up she was sure to find him near her. If she seated herself at the piano in the grand drawing-room, she would find him at her side, ready to turn the music for her. She curled her crimson lips in the deepest scorn as she looked at him. He had been untrue to the memory of poor hapless Doris. Now he would be un, rue to Vivian s memory by sunning himself in another's smiles, she told herself. "Why was Vivian not with him ?" she wondered. Then she remembered that it was not unusual for gentlemen to go abroad without their wives. No doubt Vivian had not chosen o come. There was one who looked on with darkening brow as Frederick Thornton hovered at Doris's side; one who turned away as though the sight were bitter pain to him, although he had noticed Doris did not encourage these attentions. Karl Lancaster could not endure the thought of Doris's smiling upon another. A sudden coldness sprang up between the two young men, and Karl was pleased when his father announced his intention of returning home. A fortnight later, the Lancasters took up their summer quarters at the Ocean Beach Hotel, New- port, and Doris was at once proclaimed the beauty and belle of he season. To Doris's dismay, Fred- erick Thornton followed them. Again he sought and improved every oppor- tunity of cultivating beautiful Miss Fielding's acquaintance. There was a certain dash of romance about it, owing to the fact that the girl seemed to detest and avoid him so. Frederick Thornton was by no means vain. Yet he was not blind to his own accoin; lishments, and the favour in which he was held by the charming belles who graced the beach. It was quite u•eless for bewitching young girls to single him out as the handsomest and best catch of the season. He was proof against all their pretty arts of coquetry, their coy blushes and blandishments. It was soon whisp red that he had no eyes nor ears for any one save the beauty and belle, Miss Fielding. He was not to be won, that was evident. "Why does he follow me about so persistently, I wonder ?" Doris often thouvht to herself. It often occurred to her to warn those pretty girls that the idol they were so eager to worship was married ; that he had no right to give to the world the impression that he was single—free to woo and win th, m. Mrs. Lancaster watched young Mr. Thornton's persistent wooing with anxiety for her own son's sake. Once she attempted to discover the state of Doris's heart by close questioning in regard to her ardent admirer, but Denis turned such a pale, pained face toward her that she cried out in alarm. 'Do not mention Frederick Thornton's name to me. I hate him," she said, in a quick, stifled voice: and before Mrs. Lancaster could recover from the astonishment of witnessing this vehement outburst of passion from the usually quiet Doris, the girl had quitted the room. That day a strange, reckless resolve came to Doris. She would learn to control herself better than this, that the sound of his voice, the touch of his hand, the glance of his eyes, agitated her so. it almost seemed to Doris that the whole world must read her secret. She loved hart. That afternoon, when Frederick Thornton joined a group of young girls on the sea shore, among whom was Doris, he noticed with a thrill of pleasure that she did not tarn and walk abruptly away as usual; and he flattered himself that. the wilful beauty, who had taken such an aversion to him, was beginning to look upon him more kindly. The group of chatt-ring young girls made way for him. He flung himself down on the white beach at Doris's feet; but the graceful, golden head, after a slight inclination, was turned proudly away from the face gazing up into her own. "I want you to settle a dispute for us, Mr. Thorn- ton, if you will," said a bewitching little brunette, laying a little mite of a hand, in a half-careless, half. caressing way, on his arm. "I "in trying to induce these timid girls to take a dip in the sea with me. I have already half persuaded Miss Fielding. If she goes, the rest will follow. Now, add your entreaties to mine, and tea them a bathe will be delightful, this warm afternoon." Frederick Thornton looked up in alarm. "I think Miss Fielding was quite right in hesitating to trust the- water to-day; there is danger in its wooing. Do you see how high the breakers dash on the shore? I have been told that it betokens a swift, treacherous under- current." "Oh, how cruel of you to say that, Mr. Thorn- ton I" pouted the little brunette, who was quite an expert swimmer among the breakers, and longed to show her dexterity in battling with the huge waves. "Of course your opinion will decide Miss Fielding, and my eloquent arguing of an hour's duration has been in vain.' "I think not,' returned Doris, very quietly. " I have made up my mind to go into the surf with you." The little brunette looked delighted ; Frederick Thornton looke as he felt—much anooyed. " Why do you wish to court daoger, Mi a Field- ing ?" he asked, in a low voice. "You can see for yourself how heavy the sea is. / beg ot you do Dot be_ tempo-a...lite lie env," •

div.p: TRUST IN PROVID-I'NCE, BUT KEEP YOUR POWDER DRY.

T ex- pect Providence will step in and preserve us against carelessness, or total apathy, is simple ignorance. There comes the express ; will Providence B4VP you it you remain on the metals ? The fierce fire rages in yonder stairway ; will Providence save you if you reins., the proffered ladder? The huge, majestic steamf r is last filling with water ; will Providence save you if cou I-i. lessly refuse the life-boat? The epidemic of Bright', Disease is raging around sou ; can you afford to siiiio.y trust in Providence when there is a simple, proven. sur, remedy that cures—Warner's Safe Cure ? div.head: LIVERPOOL MURDER.
div.p: THE LIVERPOOL MURDER.

The trial of William Mill r, a sailor, aged tweri.y- seven, for the murder of Edward Move, an eldei:l- - vendor of secondhand books, and the attempted muffle r of a boy named N-edham. eceased's assistant,was com- menced at the Liverpool Assizes on Monday, before Mr. Justice Hawkins. The principal witness was tne Needham, who stated the on the eveninl of the 18'• February the prisoner came into deceased's house. asked witness if he knew where deceved kept his morn., witness replying that he did not know. Deceased after wards came in and shook hands with prisoner. saving he did not expect to see him so soon. D- ceased said t witness that prisoner was the lodger he had had beff re adding that he would sleep on the sofa that night. ano the next day the bed in the best room was to b. mad. up for him. Witness went to bed, leaving prisoner and Moyse in the kitchen. Next morning, shortly after five, 1 prisoner came into witness's room carrying a lighted candle. He asked atassit a manhole over the top of the staircase, and went through it into the attic, remaining about ten minutes. He returned to witness's bedroom, blew out the candle, and struck witness on the hes,' with something. Prisoner seized him by the thrnat,and he lost consciousness. He next remembered being on 1 the kitchen floor and prisoner striking him on the head . with the poker. Prisoner afterwards put his boots and ; jacket on and Sent into deceased's room, witness hear- 1 ing him say" gord morning." He left the house after 1 threatening witness, who went into deceased's room and saw a cut on his head and blond on the pillow. Witness ran into the street and informed a dockgateman. On Wednesday the trial of Miller was concluded Tke jury, after an absence of twenty minutes, found the I prisoner guilty. In reply to the usual question why I sentence of death should not be pas,sed, prisoner fain,ly answered," Nothing more than what I have said." Sen- tence of death was then passed in the usual form, the prisoner betraying no emotion.

One of the oldestchurches in Washington has a steeple formed of a tree. The church was built under the shade of a tall poplar, and an ingenious member of the cwn- gregation suggested that the tree should become the steeple. Accordingly the poplar was deprived of itg head, the bell being hung on the stump. This is, per- haps, the only instance on record of a church spire hay- ing been made from a tree.

div.p: Doris crested her beautiful golden head, looking down at him with cold, proud eyes. She would have gone now, even if de .th itself stared her in the face, just to show him how lightly she valued his opinion. " Why do you take so much interest in thie matter?" asked Doris, sharply. The words, " Because I love you so madlYt sprang to his lips; but he forced them back. This was neither the time nor the place to utter them. He smiled, and a tender look came into his Soo dark eyes. "Would I not lift my voice, stretch out tel hands, to save a rash child from rushing headlong into danger? or turn aside from its course a bird_ that was seeming y bent upon flattering straigas into a trap? You are like the child and the bird; you must be saved from the fruits of your own folly." With a haughty toss of her golden, curly heacif Doris picked up her book and lace sunshade, as° walked away. Frederick looked thoughtfully out over the water' In that moment his mind had flown back to the har; less girl-bride who had found death in the Gold, at!!! waves. The impute., came to him to follow hhr, Fielding, and tell her the story of poor, hapless Doris. The handsome premises of M.e,;erF. Skelton wich have just been gutted were erected so late as 1887, and were therefore described as the " Jubilee" Buildings The architect was Mr, J. E. Wright. Messrs. Skelton's business had been previou•ly carried on in Buttermarket-street, but their esta,b- lishment was then very much less commodious.

div.head: TIT ASSISTANTS.
div.p: TIT ASSISTANTS.

The number of assistants employed in the shop was 30, but a large number of these were at their teas when the fire broke oat. They were quickly on the spot however wnen the news of the fire was received, and they rendered material help in saving materials, for they worked with a will. Some af the lady assistants especially are entitled to great praise, as they boldly rushed in to the shop de- spite the falling debris, and were instrumental in saving some very valuable articles. div.head: WOXEN IN BURMA.
div.p: WOXEN IN BURMA.
A HAPPY, HAPPY LAND.
What delightful creatures Burmese womert•rnust !

Rudvard Kipling in his " Mandalay " has chanted their praises as only Kipling can. Mrs. Miln has written of her far-off sisters with a chivalrous enthusiasm worthy —shall I say ?—of man. And now here is W. FL Field- ing trumpeting theirvirtues in" Black wood'sllagazine." The advocates of the emancipation of the female will be delighted t) learnthat in Burma at least, if,not in Eng- land, women !enjoy absolute freedom. Possibly they will find in this fact an explanation of the sweetness,th-e grace, and the comeliness which, by cemmon consent, are distinguishing features of the Burmese women. In this semi-civilised•State, with its curious barbaric sur- vivals, women stand on an absolute equality with men aslar as law, religion, and custom are concerned. In the face of the law man and woman are aalike. Girls share equally with boys in all inheritance, and they in- herit absolutely. l'here are no trustees 'between a woman and her property, and when she marries she re- tains it. Her husband has no control over it at all, neither has he any legal control over her. 'From her childhood up shels free. Chivalry, says Mr. Fielding, with a side thrust at our Occidental ways—chivalry, which praised women as gods and treated them as slaves, never came to Burma. No Burman lover sings his mistress as something too good for this world, and then treats her as something infinitely inferior to him- self. The women of Burma have always been held for what they are, and they have had freedom to find their own place in a very real world, unfettered by conven- tions and rules. What has bees the result? Why, this—that of all women in the world none are more womanly than she is, none possess in greater strength all the nameless attractions of a woman. She is no Helen, she is no Aspasia, least of all she is an Amazon ; but to those who know her she is everything that is lovely and desirable in womanhood. In manner she is quiet and self-restrained. She is never self-con- scious, seldom coquettish, and her voice, like Annie Laurie's, is low and sweet. Curiously enough, Burmese women have no accomplishments. They de not play any instrument, an 4 they don't dance. On the other hand—and as the Prince of JPOU would say, "That is the thing!"—they are thoroughly acquainted with house- hold matters. They can weave and cook and sew, and even as girls they look out upon the world with frank, open, clear-looking eyes. They do n 4 marry young. 'From sixteen to twenty is the usual age, but it is often gate?. . I

A pretty custom of the country is known as courting- time, Mr. Fielding's description is so charming that it .deserves to be given in full. There is a delightful custom all through Burma, an *institution, in fact, called " courting-time." It is from

He read as follows : " It is a pleasure to see so many of MIT friends here to- night,and 'I feel sure we all give them a hearty welcome, and I believe they would he a gr.itt help if they could see their way clear to become memhers of our society. You will see by the Secretary's report that the sub- scriptions are not heavy being only 11, .per month. --Th.oz:C—n-stamatt expressed the gratificition that he was sure the members felt at the kindness tat the great many wholtad come to join them in the colebration of their first anniversary. It was a pleasant thing that they were met there that night and he thought the outward appearance of the room which was not usually very graceful had been transformed hv some busy hand which they ought to be thankful to fnrmakine it look so com- fortable and cheerful. (App'anse It hardly seemed that a whole year had gone aincethe Christian Endeavour Movement began in connecti in with Wyeliffe. Looking back over the year he thought that wdh a few excep- tions they had kept in their membership those with whom they started. They had nothing very great to Chronicle and nothing Much to boast about, hut they had a great many reasons to he thankful and they were not going to despise the day of small things Small thing had led to substantial results, and tie himself thought if the members were loyal to their-pl-dge and the church with which they were identified, in course of time their fi,iciety would manifestly increase and grow. The great thing that they should exercise their minds abut, was whether they were the better for the Society meetings, land he thought they would all agreetho they were: the ' meetings had done a great deal to strengthen their own spiritual life and character. Their subject for the even- ing was " How could the endeavourers help their church." The first way wati, they could hole by simpli- city, unselfishness and consistency of/Dent-mai character. Stlcond, by diligent loyalty to all the engagements of the church. He would like to say that though they'felt they .wed a duty to the church they should like to feel that the church owed amething to their Society. div.head: SINGUAR DEATH OF A. POSTMAN.
div.p: SINGUAR DEATH OF A. POSTMAN.

On Monday morning Mr. S. Brighouse, the county clron-r, held an inqoest at the Parade Room, Irlam-st., on the body of Thomas Russell, postman. Mr. Fenna repres-nted the London and North-Westerii Railway Company. Miry Jane Russell, widow of the deceased, 38, Gee- at., Warrington, said her husband was employed at the Gmeral Post Office. She remembered that on the 14th November he get hurt on the railway. fie said he was patting the mail hags in the ,rain when a carriage door flow open and struck him on the head, cutting his eye. fie said it was between a quarter to nine and nine o'clock and he was knocked on the back of his head and b •ca me unconsci .US. The next day he went Co his work and continued for eleven days, bet during that time he was complaining about his head. Dr. Starkey Smith attended him up to his going to the Infirmary where he stayed a fortnight. From the time of Dr. Smith seeing him up to his death he never did any work. Be had always been a healthy man. D. T. Starkey Smith said the deceased came under Ihis care about a week or two before the accident. Witness saw him a day or two after the accident. He said he had ben waiting for the mails when the train Caine in with a door open. Trio door struck him on the head, dazing him About the beginning of December deceased had a seizure similar to others that he had had, and his right side, arm and leg were paralysed. Witness attended him and got Dr. Langdale, from the Infirmary, to examinedeceased. He was taken tothelnfirmary where he remained for a fortnight, after whi-h he went home.. He was sometimes only partially conscious,but in March he got so well kvi to be able to dress and walk about the room. Three weeks ago he seemed to collapse and gradually sank away until hedied on Thursday, the 9th inst. Witness and his son (Dr. R. Smith) and Dr. Lang- • dale made a post-mortem examination and found that the skud was uninjured. On removing the skull cap the left side of the brain was much different to the other. was much less and flatter. On removing the brain they found that about a third of the left half was a soft masa,alm mat like an abscess. One of the arteries supply- ing the brain was blocked by some disease, the blond being prevented from going to the brain. In answer to the coroner, Dr. Smith said he did not think that the injary eith •r aided or accelerated death. There was evidently some disease of the brain going on,causing the seizure that decease i had been subject to. He did not think that the accident had anything to do with the cause of death. He should describe the cause of death as " Embolism of the left cerebral artery."
The jury returned a verdict of " Da-'•11 from Natural Ca.uses "in accordance with the medical evidence.

div.head: -0-- A. WARRINGTON 131 J [MIER HEAVILY FINED,
div.p: -0-- A. WARRINGTON 131 J [MIER HEAVILY FINED,

William Warta Wash-lane, butcher was charged at th. Warringt m Borough Court, on M(!ndav, before Mr. F. M mks. and other magistrates, with having on Mty lst, the carcise of a cow deposited for the purpose of sale in his slaughter-house in Pemberton's yard,the same heir!, diseased and unfit for the food of man. The Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) prosecuted, and Mr. Percy Davies decenried.

In opening the case, the Town Clerk said that the charge was an offence againq section 11.6, of the Public Health Act, whi,•ll enacts that any person having dig. e .Ferl meat for sale shall be liable to be prosecuted and fined £2O or imprisoned for three months. This WN3 is very seri,ms offence, and it was his duty to call their worships' attention to a resolution passed by the H alth Committee some time ago, asking the la-rich in their discretion to send anyone committing this offonce to prison, without the option of a fine. . . .

Ralph Norman, nuisance inspector, said that on May Ist, at ten minutes to eight, he visited defendant's premises in Wash lane. He went into the slaughter- house, and on entering he saw a cow banging on side hooks, dressed, and washed, and clearred,and skewered. Reexamined it, and he was of opinion that it was unfit for human food. Woen witness called defendant's at- twition to it he repli d, " What am Ito do. You sett times are had, and there is so much opposition.' Wi- ness told him he was goin .! to seize the meat as being unfit for human food. Defendant said tat the meat was not intended for human food, but it was for boiling down for pigs, he haying given 10s. for it. Witness took the meat to the Town Hall, and had it weighed there and found it weighed 31810 s. ; the lungs weighed 281b5., and the liver 321b5., which was three times as heavy as they ought to be. Mr. Owen,. J.P., gave an order for the destruction of the meat, and it was des- troyed. When the meat was taken out at the Town H the skewers had been taken out, but the defendant ' denied that he had taken them out. Cross-examined : A Marl named Bark aonse had dress -.el the carcase. A. witness had been subncenaed to attend the court who wou'd prove th t the m at had been offered for sele,but ,he had not appeared at the court. They had heard that the wtness hal loft the town that morning. I Dr J Guest Gornall, deputy medical officer of tealth, said that he examined the carcase, and it was evidently intended for sue, because the lining membrane sur- rounding the lungs was strinped. The places were covered with tuberculosis. The lungs were separate from the body, and they were most extensively diseased. They were one mass of tutp.roules.—Cross-examined : he food might have been intended for pigs, but the carcase was dressed as though tor tiuman food. • 1 Inspector Nwell said that the carcase was dressed in the usual way for food. Mr. Davis said that this was a serious charge to bring against his client will up to the present time, he would inform the bench,had boen his (Mr. Davieslown hutchor (Laughter.) He would admit that the meat in question was the worst sample of diseased meat that he ever saw, but that was the strength of his case. The carcase was that of a cow which was badly diseased, and everybody round about knew of it, and belonged to Mr. Hewitt. Mr. Hewitt on the Ist of May offered the cow to Worrell for 10s. to be killed and the flesh boiled up for pigs. Worr nit accepted the offer, and unfortunately employed a man to dress it, who did not bear the best of charac. ters in these matters. It was no doubt foolish to take the cow into the slaughter house, but the man had had no instruction to do so. He hoped the bench would deal leniently with the defendant.
Vr. W. Pierpoint, who .at on the bench, said that du i r ng the whole time he ha.] noticed detendant he had always sold meat of a high class. He thought that should be said in defendant's favour.

Mr Monks, in giving the decision of the bench, said that they had given the eve v-Ty serious consi ler ttion, and had taken notice of all the points in derenr,ant'i favour, hut they could not do less than fine him £5 and costs, £lO in all.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT
IVONDAY.-A CONSTIL'UTIONAL "POINT."

llii the House of Commons on Monday evening Mr. LABOUCHERE drew attention to the presence of he Earl of SELEORNE (Lord W.lmer). Replying to the SPEAKER his Loroship said be was not a lord of Parliament, but he was a peer of the realm. It was not his intention to apply for ha writ of summons until the House had con- sidered whether he was not still the duly elected repre- sentative of West Edinburgh. The SPEAKER said he knew of no such claim on record as that made by the nohle Lord, and he must ask his Lordship to withdraw until the question his right to sit in the House had ben decided by the House. Lord SELBORNE accordingly withdrew. Sir W. HARCOURT then proceeded to state his view of the law on the sut j,ct, holding that on suc- ceeding to a p•erage a person became a lord of Parlia- ment and incapable of being a member of the House of Commons, and that the House being satisfied that Lord WOLMER had become a lord of Parliament, would be justified in issuing a new writ fir West Edinburgh. He , submitted that it would be convenient to refer ; to the Commit.ee now sitting, the question whether Lord Woutsa had succeeded to the Earldom of Selborne. Mr. BALFOUR agreed with the Chancellor of the Exchequer as to the law, but thought that if inq 'try was to be made it should be made by a special committee. Sir W. HARCOURT acceded to this propzisal. Mr. CURZON Wil•hed to ni.ike a few observations on behalf of Lord Skr.nortivE, ad Mr. COURTNEY also intervened, whereupon Sir W. HARCOURT said that in the circumstances he would ITIOye that a writ be issued, and the discussion could be adjourned. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN accused the Chancellor of the Exchequor of acting " iii a fit or temper." Sir W. HARCOURT retorted th,t Mr CHAMBERLAIN had forgotten himself. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said there ought to be a full and fair inquiry %colon would take into account not merely the case id Lord SELBORNE, but all similar cages which might exist at prraror or might hereafter be brought laifore them. Mr. BALFOUR said there were great constitutional auth irittes in the House who did not take his view or that of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and it would be convenient if the motion for the Com- mittee was put down as the first order for next day. Sir W. HARCOURT acquiesced in this suggestion and with- drew his motion for the issue of a writ. .

div.head: RAILWA.Y SERVANTS' CONGRESS.
div.p: RAILWA.Y SERVANTS' CONGRESS.

The annual Congress of the General Railway Workers' Union was opened at Leeds on Monday, Mr. S. H. Booth (Preston) presiding. The annual report dealt arnong4 other things with the rejection of the Employers' Lia- bility Bill and with the question of "contracting out." The President in his address said that the action taken to smash the bill was the result of a bogus agitation got up among the London and North-Western Railway men. From what he had seen he did not believe that the London and North-Western men as a body were in favour of " contracting out." A proposal was made at the Congress on Tuesday to discontinue the grant from the funds of the Union of £lO towards the salary of Mr. John Burns, M.P. After discussion the proposal was defeated by 13 votes to 9. At the meeting on Wednesday the delegates had before them a report by the organising secretary (Mr. J. Kelly), which stated that the Union was not in such a prosperous con- dition now as it was when the last Congress was held. As a trade organisation, however, the Society had met with a very considerable measure of success. It was decided, on certain conditions, to amalgamate with the Scottish Railway Men's Union, but a proposal to join the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants was neg- atied on the ground that the present was not an oppor- tune moment.

div.head: NOrES 0 61-AIVIES AND
div.p: NOrES 0 61-AIVIES AND
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

The Warrington team came out of their shell with a vengeance on Saturday, and inflicted a crushing defeat upon the powerful Manchester Club. After their dis- plays during the two previous games, it is bard to understand how Warrington managed it, but it is very singular how they always excel themselves when pitted against Manchester. They appear to have a great liking for trouncing this club.

It cannot be said that the Manchester team was a weak one on Saturday for it included no fewer than five county players so that it was stronger than usual. Tkese five were Tindall, Baker, Thomas, J. A. Maclaren and Houldsta orth, and in addition to these there was Hallam, who was invited to play for Notts this year,but declined, and it is very probable that he will play for Lancashire.

The hero of the match was the captain of the War- rington team, R. Smith, who made a capital 68 before he was most unluckily run out. Not content with this feat, in four overs, two of which were m.tidens, he took four of the Manchester wickets for only U. runs. It is generally supposed that a good batsman is a poor bowler and vice versa, but Smith showed that both batting and bowling can be done well by the same player. Hind made his first appearance in the team for this season and his diout was very successful,for although only at the wicket ZO minutes, he totted up 30 which is pretty quick scoring. J.J. Crosfield's 22 was made with- out a chance being given,and Wordsworth,Callon,Bates. and Connor also came into double figures. Connor was the most successful Warrington bowler with the excep- tion of Smith for he took three wickets at an average of 15 rune per wicket, and J. J. Crosfield took two for 37. It is to be hoped that Warrington will keep up their good form when they visit Broughton to-day, and that the season so idauspicously begun,may end with a large majority of wins.

Owing to the match on Saturday there are some re- spectable averages, and it is very probable that Dr. R. Smith, the skipper, will be the first of the team to score a htindred runs as he only requires 24 more to complete the number. There is a big gap between him and Callon, who is the nee in the number of runs scored, for he has only scored 33.

H. Hind is nominally at the ton of the averages at present, as he has an average of 30, but as he has only played in one innings, that is not as creditable as R. Smith's 28.66 for three. The following is the list of averages up to date of those who have played in two innings, and have an average of three and over :
_ Times - not Inns out runs average. R. Smith J. Callon 3 0 33 11.00 3.3. Crosfield W.Wordsworth 3 0 27 9.00 Bates G. C'arke J Bibby W. H Podstore Clark (A) Adamson

Warrington 2nd and Golborne, on two successive Saturdays have tried to settle their differences, but on each occasion time has refused to allow them. At the match at Golborne, the game was rather in favour of Golborne, but at the return match at Warrington on Saturday, the draw was decidedly in favour of Warring- ton, for with an equal number of wickets down, they had scored almost twice as many runs as Golborne. The Warrington innings commenced very disastrously, for three wickets were lost for only four runs, but England with 34. Duckworth with 30, and Crompton with 41 put a different complexion upon the game, ard with 152 for seven wickets, the innines were closed. There was however not time enough to get Golborne out, and thus a draw was the result.

The Sankey Wesleyans had the worst of a draw with Cairo-street Unity on Saturday, time coming to their assistance otherwise it is extremely probable that a bsd mark would have been made against them. Pawnall 27. Blown 15, and John Monks, 12 were responsible for the greater portion of the score for the Unity, for six of the batsmen failed to make a single run. Pownall besides being the top scorer of the match, took three wickers of nine runs so that he did very good service for his side. Taylor, die Wesleyan' captain defied all the bowling, and was not out for s capital 20 when time was called. Entwistle also did well in conpiling 11. Booth was the mostsuccessful bowler, for he took four Unity wickets for only two runs !

Bank-st. Mission met a team on Saturday known as Briggs C.C.frnm Widues,a team which will have to learn a bit of sornethinq before they do hononr to Johnnie Bergs, for I suppos.4 they call themselves after him. They were all tumbled out for 28. their highest score be- ing sevtn,while Bank-st. made 58.

Among other matches I notice that St. Ann's hal to admit the superior prowess of Bewiey-road Y.P S., although Gibson tried hard to save the match, and scored 27. Whitehouse and Jones, however. more than counterbalanced this on the other side. The Windsor Wesleyans are most unfortunate when they visit this part of the country, and on Saturday they received a good thrashing at the hands of the Penketh Wesleyans. It is very strange how ill luck dogs them, for tlify play really good cricket.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

On Saturday, Mr. J:iii;drington, the well-known Warrington rider, made a very plucky attempt to lower the twelve hours northern road record which stands at 196 i which wa2 made last season by Genrre Lascelles of the Manchester Wheelers. Waddington was riding in splendid form but for emme forty miles he was indiffer- entiv paced which proved to be really the death-blow to his attempt. • In spite of this drawback the rider covered 195 miles in the stipulated time and finished up stronv at the rate of 23 miles an hour, the last 11 miles being accomplished in 20 minutes. This speaks well for Mr. Waddington's powers and WP understand that he isgoing to have another try on Wednesday. all being favourable. Mr. Waddington was, we are asked to say, indebted to the gentlemen who gave him their services in pacing.
SWIMMING.

On Wednesday evening the Warrington water polo team went to Manchester to play Osborne Reserve there. The match was not in connection with any league,being only for the purpose of practice. A t ery good game was witnessed, and in the first half the Mancunians were leading by 8 goals to nil. The second half was of m >re even nature,Locker for Warrington scoring two,and the Osborne team one, so that the result on the termination of play was Osbortießeserve 9,Warringten 2. Warrington were singularly unfortunate in the matter 01 scorin g,for Turner made several promising shots which unfortu- nately only struck the posts. This outcome of the game is nrt considered at all discreditable, but rather other- wise, as there are only twe teams in the neighbourhood understood to he superior to the Osborne Reserve, and hose are the Osborne First and the Mayfield Polo Team,

div.head: WARRINGTON YACHT RACE.
div.p: WARRINGTON YACHT RACE.

Owing to an error on the part of the start-r in the annual yacht race in connection with the W.rrington and Bank Quay Sailing Club held on Easter Siturday wig declared null and void, and the race was ordered to be run again. On the occasion of the first race, the Pink proved to be the winner. The same eight yachts, viz., Pink, Woodcock, Silver Cloud, Maggie, Gipsy, Merlin, Siesta and Wit 'flower, again entered for the race which took place last Saturday, from Atherton's Quay to Otterspool lightship, near Garston. The day was an extremely unfavourable one for a yacht race,for th,u.e was scarcely a breath of wind, and consequently when the signal to commence was given at 2.15, some rather sarcast!c remarks about the exciting race were to be heard. A large crowd was present to witness th, start, and owing to the slowness of the progress which was made by the competitors, the spectators were able to keep pace with them along the bank, and in fact, they bad to wait for the yachts. This was not exci,ing enough,and after the first mile or two, all the crowd had vanished. It soon became evident that it would be impo +si hi,. for the greater number of the boats! to get to Garston. The , Woodcock was the first to give up, and the crew of that boat endeavoured to get as far as possible by rowing. This example was speedily followed by the remainder with the exception of the Pink, Wildfl,wer and Maggie. The Merlin came to a stop at Fiddlers Ferry, and the cre v betook themselves home. The Silver Cloud, Wood- cock and Gipsy, struggled on almost as far as Widnes, but could get no further. The Maggie managed to reach Widnes, the Wildflower which outdistanced all competi- tors at the commencement of the race, came to a stand- still at Hale Bead, while the little Pink actually reached its destination, being the only one of the eight, and it accordingly won first prizA. Wildflower taking second, and Maggie third. The whole affair was really a farce, and by no stretch of the imagination could it be called a sailing match. A drifting match, and an unsatisfactory one even at that, was all that it could be claimed to be, and it is to be hoped that the next time the event comes off, more favourible circuinstances may attend it. The owners of the three winners are respectively. Walter Warburton, Harry Warburton and Robert 8,-,rtharn. The prizes were presented to the winners on Monday evening at the Bowling Green Inn.

div.head: LADS AND LASSES AT SCHOOL.
div.p: LADS AND LASSES AT SCHOOL.

When I was a lad at school. How long ago is that ? Men whose beards are getting full of the s)rt of frost that does not thaw in the spring may love to gossip about the past, but they do not love to think of it when. alone. Oh, the infinite pathos, penitence, and heartbreak of that appealing line in Cardinal Newman's "Lead, Kindly Light"—" Remember not past years." Like spilled water, memory spreads unpleasantly when let go.

What I wint to recall now is whether my school days were my happieA,herilthitest days. The facts show clear through the mists, and the answer is No. The writer came of a sound stock, and wis well cared for, yet his greatest pains and most frequent and dangerous illnesses were when he was a lad at school. Ido not affirm this to be the rule with boys but it was so, without especial reason, with me.

And here is another man who says: " All my life,even as a lad at school, I suffered from illness. I bad dizzi- ness, violent headaches, nausea, and saw spate •floating before my eyes. S ,metimt.s I vomited a greenish-yellow fatty matter, and again was qualmish and sick without vomiting. While in my teens and up to manhood I had bilious attacks every week, more or less severe. At times I felt fairly well, and then would be taken with cold shivere, and obliged to go to bed. During each attack my appetite left me, and I could touch no food whatever. Often would I come home fiom my work and sit down. to my dinner without taking a mouthful.

"As time went on, although I was muscularly stronger, I felt a great strain on my nervous system, oppression and soreness in the head, and pain and heat behind the eyes. I felt tired and low-spirited, and got but little rest at night."

The writer's next sentence should stand by itself, like a monument. [The printer will please set it in italics.] "/n this way I continued better and worse for over thirty-four years, and what 'suffered none can imagine." _ _
Let the reader try to round up that statement in hitt mind and see how largo a fact it is, and what a lesson, it teaches.

The witness proceeds : " I underwent every sort of medical treatment and took every medicine that I heard of, but they all left llle in a short time as bad as ever. "In May, 1890, a cousin of mice, Joseph Pyke, of York, West Australia, paid us a visit and mentioned, what Mother Seigel' s Curative Syrup had done for him, when similarly afflicted ;in Australia. For a time I re- fused to try it, but being at my wit's end, I got a bottle from Mr. Frank May's store in Friar-st., and began using it. The contents of that single bottle relieved me, and I kept on with the mtcbcine in faith and hope.

"Soon all my ailments vanished. and from that time to this I have been in good health, for which my thanks are due to Mother Sigel. Her remedy it is that has built me up, and made me stronger and more energe- tic than I have been for many many years. Had I knawn of it earlier, how much misery I might have avoided. I have worked for Messrs. Huntley and Palmer. biscuit manufacturers, Reading, for thirty-nine years, and am still in their employ. Yours truly (signed) CIIMILES PYRE. 16. York Place, Chatham-st., Heading, Oatober 25ch, 1892."

What now are we to conclude from Mr. Pcke'4 ex- perience ? You see. of c.-iirae, the in ttt m .if te tt disease does its most damaging work among the young. The great majority of the human race die io coo 1,l The fittest, that is, t str4)ilge:it, iurriqe, j•isl aa Dar- win says. We fellows with the frosty beard: were ahle to fight through, and heat the diseases, the drugs, and the doctors. The weaklings fell and were ho,ied. N,xt, parents don't watch the ills of their children with half an eye. Age and maturity are blind and sellish. It is the chicks that need care and protection. If oar friead at Reading had met with Mother Seigers Curative Syrup in boyhood—hut alas ! it was not in existence „then. It is to be had note, Iviwever, and it there are many pained and suffering children, who is to blame P Answer us that.

' A ConstitutionaiTHE House of Lords has Buffered 9 ' Question. serious loss of prestige during the present week. And the worst of A is the blow has been itilcted by the hands of its reptited friends. The distressing event Waft brought about under the following circumstsoee6" Lord Worsens is one of those Liberal Unionist, who cannot so far as their action on all politic!' subjects is concerned be distinguished from 06 bluest of blue Tories. In all such questions 88 defence of the House of Lords and the Welsh ' Church he has, in fact, been apparently prepare" to go almost beyond the limits of Toryism. it , now appears, however, that his admiration for th'ew occupants of, the Gilded Chamber is of a Ore; platonic description. He is willing to suelo" them in all their absurd claims and priveleges" from a distance, but as for becoming one of thl: selves he shrinks back from the prospect wit' kind of horror, as though translation to the I:IPPer House were the commencement of a life-leeg political exile. Oti the recent death a the eminent lawyer, Lord SELBORNE, Lord Woesesse the eldest son, of course succeeded to the title and to the right to sit in the House of Lords. He accepts the peerage, but he claims that he is entitled to retain his seat in the H°llB° of Commons and to refuse to sit in the House of Lords In this action he is backad up b °IT y 1" RZON and one or two other young men vill° , upon the death of their fathers will find the- selves in the same position as lord Wertatza. .rbe • House of Corntnons has, therefore, had forced 00 ,11 it •the duty of settling a fine constitutiossi take point, and it has appointed a Committee to evidence and advise it upon the subject. ° doubt it will act upon the report of this Conon"- tee and Lord WOLAf RR will then either haVe,r retire to the obscurity of the hereditary or he will be allowed to establish a new precede° by remaining as the representative of one °I divisions of Edinburgh in the House of Cornoi°"". Liberals may view the result, whatever it nial with philosophic equanimity. But not so i'"`", Tories. With them the question is one of vitaci importance. If the ablest, the most energetic e 13,0 the most ambitious of the young peers call reit%. i in the House of Commons after the death of t'os—t fathers, as they will most assuredly do cases when they have a free choice, what is t,,°,v, come of that "pillar of the constitution 'c° . House of Lords ? Even under present, c.relleg.. stances that House is gradually falling t° llies lect, not to say contempt. If the tittle C° when it is recruited only by those aged veterweo whose day is past or by those younger men the have not the ability to make their NraY 10 it more stirring arena of the House of Comui°;:tr is bound to rapidly lose all its credit as trolling branch of the legislature. These are Con- siderations which the Tories cannot,and inded not, ignore at the present time, and therefore : sx', their responsible leaders have strongly against the claims of Lord Womize. A SUCCESSFUL RUNCORN EXHIBIT.

A gold medal has been awarded to the United Alkali Company for their exhibit at the International Health Exhibition held at Manchester last week. The caee con- tained specimens of Cashmere, Carbolic, and ordinary household soaps which had been manufactured at the Camden Works, Runcorn ; and also soda from the Run- corn Works, together with manganate of soda from the Widnes Alkali Works.
