div.head: Ruwcoux.
div.p: Ruwcoux.

Professor R. W. Handley presided at the organ of the above place of worship, on Sunday. In the morning he played—Adagio, organ Aonata No. 1 (Mendelssohn)' Andante Tranquillo, organ Sonata No. 3 (Mendelas din), March, composed and dedicated to the Runcorn Votun- teers (R. W. Handlry). In the evening, after the service the same gentleman gave the following programme Tranmere " Day Dreams" (Schumann), Grand March in G (Smart), a Muiette, b Cradle song (Kinross), " Halle- lujah Chorus" Messiah (Handel). Proiessor Handley is organist of the Church of Scotland, Liverpool, and secretary to the Liverpool Choral Society. The choir also sang with effect Sir George Elvey's anthem "Praise the Lord."

div.head: RUNCORN BOATMAN DROWNED AT MANCHBSTER. • –
div.p: A RUNCORN BOATMAN DROWNED AT MANCHBSTER. • -

An inquest was held at the City Corourr's Court, Manchester, on Friday, by Mr. Smelt, on the body of Albert Cotton, 23, a canal boatman, who had lived in Stanley-st.,Runcorn. The previous morning the deceased was with the boat he worked on at the swing bridge lock of the Rochdale Canal, near Ten Arch-lane, Manchester. He had gone on in advance to get the lock ready, and when the boat arrived he was missei. His hat was found in the water, and his body was subsequently recovered with the aid of drags. A verdict of found drowned was returned. The funeral took place at the Runcorn Ceme- tery on Monday afternoon. CHILD RIJN OYER AT RIINCMIN.

On Friday afternoon, about four o'clock, the four- year-old daughter of Ms. Ralsworth, of 18,Ashridge-st., sustained injuries by being run over. The child was in Bridge-st., when two traps were coming in orposite directions. In getting out of the way of one she stepped in front of that belonging to Mr.W.hallerof 23, Church- st., which was loaded with potatoes at the time, and although the driver made every effort to pull up, the little one was knocked down, and a wheel passed over her body. She was promptly picked up and was after- wards examined by Dr. Robinson. No bones were found to be fractured,biat it was feared she bad received internal injuries. THE ELECTION OF A PARISH COUNCIL AT CLIFTON. The election of a Parish Council for the small town- ship of Clifton took place en Saturday. Mr. John Row- land, acted as returning officer. There are but 40 effec- tive voters on the parochial register, arid of this num- ber 27 voted, several having removed since the issue of the register. There were nine candidates,seven of whom were present at the subsequent counting of the votes. The result of the election was as follows :—Elected— Joseph Stokes, The Grange, Clifton, 19 votes ; John Wilson, Oxford-road, Runcorn, 17 votes ; William Fletcher, Mersey View, Clifton, 16 votes ; Peer Massey, Mersey View, Clifton, 13 votes ; and William Weston View, Clifton, 13 votes. Not elected—Samuel Rowland, John Cundy, William Pope,and John Thomas. A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the returning officer, on the proposition of Mr. Joseph Stokes, seconded by Mr. Peter Massey. CAMDEN WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—THE REOPENING SERVICES.

On Sunday this chapel was reopened. During the period it has been closed great improvements have been effected, and the saared edifice now presents a bright and cheerful appearance. The painting and decorating have been efficiently executed by Mr.Jarnes Green. The cost of the work, together with sanitary improvements, is estimated at about £7O. Through the liberality of Mr. Speakman, a new rostrum, in conformity with the old One which is now being used by the choir, was utilised for the first time. The preacher was 1/Ir. F. 0. Moston, of Lymrn,who formerly carried on business in Runcorn, and identified himself with Camden Chapel. The dis- course was very much appreciated. In the afternoon the same gentleman gave an address to parents and scholars. Special anthems were sung by the choir,under the conductorship of Mr. Batley, and the orchestra was assisted by Miss Temperley, Mr. C. Ditetifold, and Mr. Arthur Dutton, violinists. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. In connection with this Sunday school, the anniver- sary services were held on Sunday, and were of a most successful character. The preacher for the occasion was the Rev. W. Wright,of Nantwich,and he ably discoursed to large congregations. At the morning service he spoke specially tc Christian workers and Sunday school teachers, and in the evening he gave some valuable advice to young men. Mr. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C., presided at the,afternoon gathering when special hymns and anthems were sung. An appropriate address was delivered by the pastor of the church, the Rev. T. 13rainall. In the anthem " I will praise my Maker." Miss Davies, Miss Stubbs, Mr. Parry, and Mr. Ambrose Shingler gave the quartette, and duets were given by Miss Wilson and Mr. Herbert Woodward, and Miss Hil- lidge and Mr. R. flillidge. Mr. Gittens, jun., ably pre- sided at the organ. Collections wire taken at each ser- vice on behalf of the Sunday school and realised £22 55., which together with a sum of a little more than £l7 raised in the Sunday school, makes a total of nearly £4O.

div.head: BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.
div.p: BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.

The member l attending this Band of Hope with a few friends and workers were provided with an excel- lent repast in Brunswick-street schoolroom on Monday evening. Mr. T. Lea generously supplied the tel. The room was tasetefully decorated for the occasion by Mr. and Mrs. Nancollis. About 80 children sat down to tea, and the tables were presided over by tne following ladies : Miss C. Littler, Mrs. Eden, Mrs. Bisbrown, and Mrs. Nancollis. Amongst the friends present were Messrs. T. Lea, A. It. Norman, D. Bisbrown, E. Taylor, T. White, T. Cooke, Higgins, Jeffery, and Green. After tea a quantity of sweets was distributed. Mr. A. H. Norman proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Lea for his generosity in providing the tea. Mr. E. Taylor seconded the proposition and Messrs. D.Bisbrown and F. Cooke supported. Mr. Lea in response spoke of the pleasure it had given him to give the tea. The children then adjourned to the playground where various games were indulged in.
RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.

Mr. W. Carroll presided at a meeting held in connec- tion with the Runcorn Football Club in Mr. Riley's cafi, Bridge-street. The meeting was called for the purpose of receiving nominations for the various offices. Mr. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C., was again nominated for the position of president. The other nominations were as follows :—Captain, Ist team, W. Faulkner, G. Robin- son, S. Houghton, and S. Abra:ns ; captain, 2nd team, J. Lightfoot, and T. Antrobus ; vice-captain, 2nd team, W. Gregory, E. Woodward, T. Antrobus; and A.Clarke ; secretary, J. E. Langshaw ; assistant secretary, J. Ellison ; treasurer, C. Pownall ; committee,W. Carroll, W. Jones, A. Lightburn, S. Abrams, T. Moores, H. Cawley, W. Faulkner, W. Becke‘t, G. Robinson, E. Key, J. Goodwell, J. Fraser, H. Farmer, T. Warder, S. Houghton. H. Hughes, D. Lightfoot, E. Gregory, 0. Dunhavin, J. Mclieuzie, T. Robinson, T. Auderton, J. Stubbs, R. Moore, and G. Shaw ; auditors, E. Lunt, and T. C. Cooper ; touch judge, first team, J. Sherlock and J. Stubbs ; touch judge second team, J. Stubbs, J. Nickson, and G. Moores. It will be seen that at the forthcoming annual meeting elections will take place for several of the offices.
PEERS' ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETT.-RUNCORN AND DISTMICr

On Monday evening the sixth annual general meeting of the Runcorn and District "Peers" Economic Building Society was held at the Society's office, High-street, Runcorn. There was a fair attendance, and Mr. J. J. Speakman presided. Thera were also present —Messrs. J. K. Digges, George Burrows, William Speechley, T. H. Annett, William Bankes, G. W. Allen (solicitor), and F. W. Smith (secretary). The Chairman proposed that the balance sheet as presented be passed,which was seconded by Mr. Bankes, aud receiving a unanimous vote, was adopted. The Chairman said he was glad to be in a position to say that although the year had been adverse to their doing much business they had managed to keep the balance on the right side. On the motion of Mr. J. K. Digges, seconded uy Mr. T. H. Annett, the following gentlemen were unanimously re-elected as directors : Messrs. W. Bankes, E. Burrows, J. K. Digges and J. J. Speakman.—On the motion of Mr. Digges, seconded by Mr. Speechley, Messrs. •Lightburn and Jones were elected as members' auditors.—'l'he Chairman in propos- ing a vote of thanks to the 9.2cretary passed an euiogium on the manner he bad performed the duties of his office. This was seconded bv Mr. Annett, and was unanimously agreed to. Mr. Smith proposed, and Mr. Alien seconded, a vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was carried easaimetudy.—The Emoting then terminated.

FIER NEAR RUNCORN. The thatched roof of a cottige occupied by Mr. Finch, on the farm of Mr. Finch, Astmoor Farm, n3ar Runcorn' Wai on Wednesday morning destroyed by fire. A spark from the chimney is attributed as the cause of outbreak. THE LOCAL 'VETO PETITION FROM RUNCORN Ttie secretary of tne HiLicorn Nonconformist Minis- ters' Association has received a letter from Mr. J. T. Brunner, Ml'., in answer to the petition in support of the Local Veto Bill which was forwarded to him. Mr. Brunner states that he will have much pleasure in pre- senting it to the House of commons as it is in full ac- cord .with his views on the important subject. BRUNSWICK STREET WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. Mr. E. Taylor, senior superintendent at Brunswick-st. Wesleyan Snatchy school, presided at a meeting of the teachers aid officers on Wednesday evening. Business in reference to the Whitsuntide arrangements was trans- acted, after which a social gitnering was held. Ad- ' dresses on the importance of Sunday school work were delivered by Messrs. D Bisbrewn, J. Berkett, J. D. Jones, and P. Lawtin. It was stated that it was im- possible to estimate the value of Sunday school work, and instances were given showing the far reaching power of Sunday schJols. A coffee supper was served provided by Mr. NbUCOIIiS. The meeting, which wasa most interesting one, was well attended. PRIMITIVE MKTIODIST CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOUR CLASS,

At the meeting of this Class, on Wednesday evening, the Rev. T. Braman gave an address on " How can we endeavourers help our church ?" The annual business meeting was afterwards held. The Rev. T. Brainsll was re-elected president ; Messrs. J. WilSoll and W. Richard- son,vice-presidents ; Messrs. David Williams and Samuel Dutton, secretaries ; Miss Wilson, corresponding secre- tary ; and Miss Miles, treasurer. Maanuan's CHURCH, RUNCORN. On Monday evening an entertainment was given in the above church. The chair was occupied by Mr.,By- field and the programme was provided by Mr. T. Woods concert party. The entertainment consisted of songs, recitations, readings, humor.us and tyrolese songs and these were given in an excellent manner by the follow- ing : Misses Foster, and Marsh, Masters Banner, Cooper, Hazlenurst, and T. THE DIVING CRAZE.—LEAP FROM RUNCORN BRIDGE. About a quarter past five on Wednesday night" Pro- fessor "Lloyd. of But hport, successfully performed the feat of diving into the Manchester Ship Canal from Run corn Bridge, a height 01 75 feet. The matter was kept a profound secret and he had no difficulty in gaining admittance to the bridge. The man was dressed in a blue serge suit. Some delay was occasioned in the per- , frrmance ot the feat in consequence of a number of barges passing along tl.ie canal at the time, and during the interregnum a number of persons gathered on the bridge and near the canal. The dive is described by the spectators as a "beautiful " one and was performed wi.hout the slightest injury to the participant. A boat was in readiness which convelied him to land, and he at once p -oreeded to the Bridge Inn, Ashridge-street. THE FORTHCOMING SUNDAY SCHOOL SCHOLARS TREAT. On Tuesday evening a meeting of the representatives of the Nun-conformist Sunday schools was held in Bruns- wick-street Wesleyan vestry when the arrangements for the t rcat to scholars at Whitsuntide were under discus- sion. The chair W4S occupied by Mr. G. H. Kirkham and representatives were present from each institutiGn. It was decided to have the usual procession which is to start at 1 30. A sub-committee was appointed for the purpose of procuring a suitable field in which the scholars might subsequently play in. Messrs. Harrop and Lunt were selected as marshalls. Mr. Halford, the secretary, was thanked for his past services and be was asked to retain the positicn for another year which will be the 15 h in succession. Mr. Halford thanked the meeting for the c,,mpliment accorded to him, and acceded to the request to retain the secretaryship. A vote of thanks to tbe Chairman, concluded the meeting. DEMONSTRATION. '

There will be a grand circuit demonstration at Overton Hills, PrOdshatn, on Wednesday next, con- ncted with the Preston Brook circuit of the Primitive Methodist Connexion. The Rev. Danxy Sheen, of Sheffi,ld, will 'Peach in the afternoon and will also deliver a lecture on the "Rev. C. H. Spurgeon, his conversion, career and coronation." A public tea will be provided at 4.30.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
Tai TRANSFERENCE OF THE WESLEYAN SCHOOLS.

A special meeting of the School !Board was held on Thursday evening. Mr. J. Pritchard occupied the chair and there were also present :—Rev. Canon Wood, Rev. Dr. Crastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Mr. S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., Mr. E. unison, J.P., Mr. T. Handley, J.P., and Mr. Lake (solicitor), and Mr. Moss (clerk). The matters were dis- cussed in private for one hour and a half, and when the reporters were admitted the following resolutions were moved._

The Chairman moved the following resolution "Resolved that the offer to transfer the Wesleyan Gran- vile-st. schools) to the Board contained In Mr. Burton's letter of the 10th inst. to Mr. Lake be, and the same is hereby accept-d, and that the necessary forms be signed by the Clerk and solicitor to the Board and forwarded to the Education Department." He said the matter had been surrounded with exceptional difficulties and had taken a long time and a vast amount of consideration to over- come and r.ot without a personal struggle with the Education Department. These, however, had now been surmounted although a long delay had occurred. In July last it was coosidered that the negotiations were at an end and the Board were on the look out for a fresh site. In November last a further communication was received from the managers of the Wesleyan schools and negotiations were again resumed and proposals were again considered, and submitted to the Education Department. After considerable delay the difficulties had been removed so that n iw they were in a position to move this transfer.—Dr. McDougall in seconding the motion said he thought it was a very happy termination of what was a very considerable di:ficulty. He thought they had reason to be thankful to the managers of the Wesleyan schools that they had seen their way to act as they had done and deal with the Board and the public in such a magnanimous way. The Rev. Canon Wood moved, Mr. Taylor seccaided, and it was resolved " That the offer to sell the house and cottages adjoining the Wesleyan (Granville-street schools) contained in Mr. Burton's letter to Mr. Lake on the 10th inst , be and the same is hereby accepted, sub- ject to the ground rent being apportioned between this and the adjoining schools according to the area. The contract referred to being subject to the approval of the Education Department and to each party paying their own costs." _

..... . The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi moved, and Mr. Handley se- conded the following resolution which was passed ; That the offer to let the Brunswick-st. schools, furni- ture and apparatus contained in Mr. Burton's letter to Mr. Lake of the 19th March be, and the same is hereby accepted the tenancy to he for one year from the Ist July next, and after the expiration of such year to be determined by three months' notice in writing at any date on either side." _

Mr. Imison proposed, Dr. McDougall seconded, and it was resolved. " That subject to the Wesleyan schools being transferred to the Board in pursuance of the fore- going resolutions the Board will take over the teaching staff as a temporary arrangement at the same remunera- tion they are receiving during the current year."

THANICS TO MR. BRUNNER. The Chairman said they were all aware of the diffi- culties that had surrounded the question, and how they almost came to a standstill with the Education Depart- ment. He (the chairman) requested Mr. Brunner to obtain an interview with the D..partment, which he was good enough to do, and otherwise took considerable interest in the matter. He accompanied him on the occasion of the interview and assisted in bringing the matter to a successful issue. He therefore moved that the thanks of the Board be passed to Mr. Brunner tor his'assistance.—Dr. McDougall seconded the motion,and said the chairman was also deserving of the thanks of the Board and he suggested that his name be joined with the motion.—The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi supported the proposition. He said the action of the two had resulted in a most satisfactory settlement. The resolution was put by Dr. McDougall and carried.—The Chairman suit- ably replied, and the meeting concluded.

div.head: • IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT, Continued from page 3. THURSDAY.
div.p: • IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT, Continued from page 3. THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons on Thursday evening Mr. Saaw-LitrEvas, replying to a question put by Mr. Krzowtss, said the report of the Tuberculosis Commis- sion appeared to point to the expediency of extending the inspection of slaughterhouses, dairies, and butchers' shops, and possibly to the general establishment of public slaughter-houses. Mr. HERBAGE: asked when the Governmont proposed to go on with the Local Veto Bill, and Sir W. HARCOURT replied, " As soon as I think it consistent with the busi- ness of the House." • Sir J. T. HIBBERT obtained leave to bring in a Bill to amend the Friendly Societies Act. It proposed to enable ju eenile societies to amalgamate with adult societies, to allow societies to admit members at one year of age,and to enable provision to be made for old-age pensions. The second reading was put down for the 17th June. The second reading of the Fin411,,0 Bill having been formally moved, Mr. J. LOWTHER called attention to the depression in agriculture, and moved as an amendment that the beer duty should be readjusted with a view to the relief from taxation ot home grown uarley and hops. Mr. HENEACIR seconded the amendment. sir W. HAR COURT said the real meaning of the amendment was another 3d. on the income tax. After a shot eneral discussion on the budget proposals,in which Mr.Goscrmie and Sir W. HARCOURT took part, the bill was read a second time amid cheers.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNG° RN. 13T OUR RUNCORN CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNG° RN. 13T OUR RUNCORN CORRESPONDENT.

It is gratifying to note Runcorn's immunity from crime which has been noticeable for some time now. Last Monday the only case for hearing at the Petty Sessions was a school attendance case,and there was very little more business transacted at the previous week's session. Taken on the whole for the present year the number of cases tried have few, and these chiefly of a trivial nature. This gives an emphatic denial of a remark made by a prominent member of the Cheshire Standing Joint Committee that Runcorn was a black spot on the Mersey. This Mr. Philip Speakman, J.P., CC,. rightly repudiated at the time, and present events prove the injustice of the remark. Of course when the hip Canal was in course of construction Run- corn did receive several unwelcome visitors who did not uphold the good character which was polsessed by the inhabitants. But since they have left the town, Police Court business has shown a marked decrease, and it is to hoped this may be long maintained.

Those who are anxiowdy waiting for the work to be started which the Ship Canal Company are about to carry out at Runcorn, will be glad to know that during the week the work to be executed at Messrs. Brundrit's old yard has been commenced. This de- partment is under the control of Mr. F. Wiswall, C.E. With regard to the work of erecting four timber jetties, three dolphins, and a timber stage, together with railway sidings on the southerly side of the Canal, contracts have been invited for the erection of such. The estimate.; are to be in by the end of the month, and shortly afterwards it may be expected that the work will be put in hand. Con- sidering the present state of trade in the town this additional means of employment should be most welcome. a . _

To-day there is to be a meeting of the directors of the United Alkali Company and it will then ba decided—or should be—what is to be their future action with regard to their works at Runcorn. Last week there was published in the "Examiner" a memorial which has been submitted to the direc- tors by the local Trades and Labour Council, which has a membership of over 1,500. The memorial ex- presses regret and alarm at the rumours which have been current as to the probable closing of the works in the I .icality and expresses the hope that the town will be saved from the threatened calamity. This is the second memorial which has been sent from °Runcorn, and it. is anxiously hoped in ,tiviny quar- ters that the directors will see their way clear to increase the output at their luncorn works.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL.

Mr. J. Mclntyre, J.P., occupied ehe chair at the fort- nightly meeting of this Council held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday afternoon. There were also present Messrs. J. Knowles (vice-chairman), J. Brandreth, H. falbot, J.P., T. Baxter, C.C., H. E. Heywood, J. M. Williams,T. Lewis, T. Wright, S. Wooeward, E. Aaron, W. Bradford, C. Mounfield, C. Roylance, W. Holt, T. Darlington, J. Darbyshire, J. Weir, J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk), J. Farrington (nuisance inspec- tor), J. Swinton and W. Diggle (surveyors), and Dr. Adams (medical officer). A SHIP CANAL AGREEMENT.

Mr. Roylance stated that there was an agreement existing between the late Deresbury Highway Board and the Manchester Ship Canal Company, that if anything happened on the roads through the carelesshess of the company they were responsible. Already several acci- dents had occurred and damages had been paid. He wished to know whether the Council would have the same agreement with the Canal Company.—lt was stated that the Council would have all the power and privileges held by the Daresbury Highway Board.

HiLSBY WATER SUPPLY. Mr. James Brandreth, of Helsby House, Helsby,wrote stating that on a small property he had on fielsby Hill, he had s nk a well 75 feet deep and a bore hole 130 feet deep, and had , met with a good spring of watm.. He had had an engine pumping from it for three days at the rate of 300 gallons per hour and could not reduce the supply. Mr. ',Arrington had taken a sample of the water to test its quality. Mr. Brandreth added that he would have more water than he required and he asked the consent of the Council to lay a pipe in the road about 400 yards long from Mr. Uriffith's new house to the boundary of Alvanley to enable him to supply Mr. Griffiths and his neighbours. He would give an under aking to make good all damage to the road Em.—Mr. Heywood moved that subject to the analysis of the water being satisfaczory, the consont asked for Ise given.—Mr. Williams seconded, and the proposition was carried. THE ROADS AT WESTON.

At a meeting of the committee appointed to consider and report upon the .Southsroad and Post Office-road, Weston, held at the Dock Hotel, Weston Point on Fri- day the 3rd of May, Mr. Joseph Stokes presided, and there was present Messrs. E. Aaron, Chadwick, Wright, Diggle (surveyor), Farrington (nuisance inspector), and J. Ashton (Clerk to Rural District Council). The com- mittee inspected the roads and after full consideration it was resolved that steps be taken to compel the levelling, paving, metalling, flagging, channelling, and making good of such streets and the Bewaring of such parts thereof as are not already sewered and for such purpose that application be made to the Local Government Board to declare that the provisions contained in the Private Street Works Act, 1892, shall be in force in the contributory place of ‘v-ston and to invest the Rural District Council of Runcorn with the powers, rights, duties, capacities. liabilities and obligations which an Urban Authority may acquire by the adoption of the said Act.—lt was turthe,r resolved that the Clerk of the Runcorn District Council enquire of Messrs. White and Maclver whether the terms of the lease of the land be- loneing tc Captain Clarke are such as justified him in enclosing a portion of the street in front of his gardens. —Mr. Aaron, in moving the adoption of the report, said the question had been under discussion for 18 or 20 years b) various bodies.—Mr. Wright said as one of the deputation of the Council on the matter he seconded the motion. He thought it was time that something was done in the matter.—The motion was carried,

div.head: GREAT EIIDWORTH WATER WETLY.
div.p: GREAT EIIDWORTH WATER WETLY.

The Committee appointed to deal with this subject had resolved that sutij.ct to the sanction of Mr. Piers Egerton Warburton of Arley being obtained to the aSiRg of the present water supp'y as a motive power, and to the water being taken from the spring at the foot of the hill, an engineer be instructed to prepare a scheme for supplying the village of Great Budworth with water from such spring.—The Clerk (Mr. Aahton) informed the Committee that a water rent could be charged suffi• ciently high to defray all costs , of the supbly.—The Chairman in submitting the report moved that the matter be referred to the Pariah Co3ncil and Mr. War- burton for their consideration. —Mr. Baxter seconded, and the motion was carried.

div.head: WATER_SUIPPLY OF WESTON.
div.p: THE WATER_SUIPPLY OF WESTON.

Mr. Aaron asked that Mr Farri»gton give the Council his report on the water supply of Weaton.—Mr. Farring- ton said he had made a visitation of houses at Weston with respect to the water supply. He found that there was a very intermittent supply and he served notices upon twenty owners which effected 88 houses. For some time afterwards the water supply was im- proved, but it was now no better at all. In many instances they had not got a drop of water upon the premises. They drew their supply frarn the Run- corn Urban District Council's mains.—Dr. Adams said that on the occasion of one of his visits to Weston ha found there was no pressure. He tried to fill a bucket but had to give up the attempt. He had recommended a better water supply in his last two annual reports Mr. Farrington said the Runcorn Urban Council collected water rents from the residents at Westrin, althmigh they failei to supply the water. They took proceedings against Mr. Aaron some time ago.—Mr. Aann said he was in Weston before the water wlrk4 were commenced and after it was fvrmed the supply was never as had since the Runcorn Commissioners took the water works ever. Last year they had a ratepayers' meeting at Weston and five or six of the residents were delegated to meet the Commissioners. They were very well received, and for some weeks they were well served with water. Since the frost they could get no water supply at all I except they remained up until midnight. They could get no redress whatever.—The Chairman said there was sufficient evidence to show that the water supply of Weston was very deficient, and he thought the Clerk should be instructed to draw the attention of the Run- corn Urban District Council to the subject 'asking them what they intended doing.—r. Aaron said that would meet with his wishes. He would propose that the Clerk write to the Urban Council drawing their attention to the inatter.—Mr. Woodward seconded the proposition, and it was carried. TRH MEDICAL OFFICER'd REPORT. . .
Dr. Adams in his report stated that there was a large diminution of infectious diseases throughout the district. —The report was adopted. PLANS.

The following plans were approved of :-24 houses proposed to be erected in Cawdor-st., Stockton Heath, by Mr. C. W. Davenport; 3 houses proposed to be ere ited in Chester-road, Stockton Heath, by Mr. C. W. Daven- port ; additions and alterations proposed to be made to houses at Weston Point by the Weaver Navigation. . THE OCCUPATION Or HOUSES AT WALToN INFERIOR. A letter was read having reference to the oceupation Of certain new houses at Walton Inferior, which it was stated had been done in ignorance without occupation certificates. The explanation was considered satisfac- tory and it was decided that no proceedings be taken. On the recommendation of the Inspector a certificate of occupation was granted. A DILAPIDATED correan. _ . . .

The Medical Officer ot Health reported upon the can• ditiontof a dilapidated cottage at Walton InTerior, and the Inspector was directed to cointnuuicate with the owners in reference thereto. This was all the business.

div.head: LIVERPOOL WESLEY AN SYNOD.
div.p: LIVERPOOL WESLEY AN SYNOD.

During the present week, the Liverpsol Wesleyan Synod has been held in the Bold-et. Wesleyan Church, Warrington, and as a consequence there has been a very large influx of Wesleyan ministers and prominent lay- men into the town. The meetings during the day have been reserved to the ministers and delegates, but the evening meetings have been open to the public,and they have been very successful. TEMPERANCE MEETING.

The meetings were ceminenced on Monday evening, when a temperance meeting was held in the Bold-st. We- sleyan Church. There was a good attendance.—The Rev. Charles GARRETT, chairman of the Liverpool District, presided, and he was supported on the pletforro by the Revs. J. Elitism, Owen Watkins, G. D. Mason, H. Bone, H. B. Workman, M.A., and W. Briscombe. The CHAIRMAN in his opening speech after a humor- One allusion te an attack of influenza to which be had been subject, said that he came to that meeting with feelings of the liveliest gratitude. It was a marvellous sign of the times. He remembered the time—for he was considerably older than the temperance movement— when a temperance meeting could not be announced in any Wesleyan Chapel in the land. He remembered the time when a little handbill announcing a band of hope was carried surreptitiously, not by the stewards, into the pulpit and placed there to let the congregation know that a band of hope meeting was to be held on the following Tuesday. He remembered the minister entering the pulpit and see- ing the bill, and the orthodox superintendent of to-day would not have been filled with such surprise if he had seen a bill announcing a socialistic meeting to be held in a neighbouring place on the coming Tuesday. The minis- ter in question actually saw lying on the pulpit an an- nouncement that there was to be a band of hope meet- ' ing looked at it,held it up as if there was some delusion, I ' and then tore it in shreds, flung it down, put his toot upon it, and then went on with the service. (Laughter.) Ile (Mr. Garrett) did not speak about it in anger. When he looked back to that, and remembered that that night and during the week, there would be temperance meet- ings not just announced, but held in Wesleyan Chapels I all over tie country, commencing in Wesley's Chapel in 11 I London. City.road chapel he thought the movement I had made marvellous progress in his own life-time. In I 1832 at Church-st, Preeton,no one would have expected the seven uninfluential men to have made such a tremen- dous change in the public feeling of the country. They were '6 nnteedys." but it was rarely that the " some- body's " did anything. (Laughter.) At that time every- body believed in drink and that it was indispensible, bat he must congratulate his audience upon the 'Change which had taken place in the habits of the people. The drink traffic had been shaken to its centre. The State regarded it as a kind of ticket of leave thing and hesit- ated to renew its license. (Laughter.) The trade was terribly frightened at the Local Veto Bill, and were actively' fighting it, but he believed that with God's aid, the temperance cause will ultimately be victorious. The Rev. H. B. WORKMAN. MA., said that his grand- father was a brewer and had 20 tied houses. Be cut off his (the speaker's) father with a shilling because he was almost the first teetotaler in the Wesleyan ministry. His father at Didshury was the only student in the college who did not drink a glass of beer, and when he joined the Alliance, the governors of the college called him before the disciplinary meeting of the college because he had joined such a dreadful political institution. He (the tipraker) was certain that it would be difficult to find any young man in the college now who ever had a glass of beer. This was a strong proof of the temperance movement. (Applause). HIS text that night was the following resolution "That this meeting, convened by the te vernonl district synce,expresses its gratification at the introduction of the Liquor Traffic Local Control Bill, and teesta every effort will be made to secure the pass- ingot the measure during the present session of her Majestee Government." (Applause.) He wished there was more enthusiasm throughout England on behalf of that bill. They had come to the parting of the ways, and were in a very critical position, and required the enthusiasm and support of all the Christian people of the enurtrv. (Applause.) All people, all the churches and political parties should de all in their power to concen- trate their thnnghts to procure the passing of the bill. They must endeavour to route the conccience of the cenntry. He knew that there were some people who ' nhjected to some of the provisions of the bill. Some ob- jected to it because the movement, they said, was poli- tical. Tie had no sympathy with that objection. This was a great religious and moral movement, and the fact that the Bill as proposed from the Government bench, did not make it political. It only showed that the moral and religious movement had reached the highest quar- ters, that a government should try to carry it out. He thought that the Methodist Church had not been poli- ticel enough in the past. Had it been so, many more meaeuree for the uplifting of the people would have been Passed, and Methodism itself would be much more powerful to-day. it was also said that the bill would not snlve the question thoroughly. He would like to know how long they were geing to wait, if they were to have a perfect measere. He, himself, believed that it was better to have half a loaf than none at all. To those who objected that it was not moderate enough, he would say that it was a very moderate bill, in fact, too moder- ate for him in some reapects. Re would like to have had the club' included, end they must also be careful as to what was meant be hotels. There was a great number of itehemee before the country, but he considered that local option was the fundamental principle at tke bottom of all of them. With regard to compensation, he would not givee the brewers any further compensation than the time limit. in every business, the persons engaged carried it on krowiree the risks, and running the risks, and he did not see why the brewers and publicans should have exceptional treatment in this matter. To be per- fectly fair, if there were any publicans who had invested their everything in the public-house, he would be willing to treat them differently. Thii was not the case in the great majority nf instances however. The public-houses were the pp-minty of the+ great brewers and the publicans were liable to be turned out at a week's notice. He did not believe in the brewers having two businesses. Let them lrvk after their brewing. (Applause.) In conclu- sion, he hoped that the country would support the bill with enthusiasm, and though they might not pass it this year. they were certain to carry it some day or other. (Anplaneee The Rev. W. BRISCOMBE supported the resolution. He believed that the passing of the Local Veto Bill would be of immense advantage to the country. The countries where the best legislative work was done were always the most prosperous, and therefore he welcomed the bill heceuse he believed that it promoted benevolent legislation. It was because he believed that temperance legislation W3B of such benefit to the country that he was willing to sunpnrt any measure which promoted temperance, end he was willing to accept even a (ruler of a loaf rather than not get anything at all. (Annleneei The Rev. Mixer BONE supported the motion. He acid there ought to be a check put upon the House of Lords in their action with such measures as the Local Veto Bill. When this hill was passed,the drink question would not be settled, but would only enter upon a new Phase. They shonld bring their influsnce to bear upon the House of Commons and. House of Lords in favour of the Local Veto Bill which had been introduced by her , Majesty's Government. The Methodist Church had great influence in the country, and its influence in favour of that bill would be a great aid in its passing. (Annlause.) The resnlutinn was passed unanimously, and the meet- ing terminated with the pronouncing of the benediction.

div.head: TUESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: TUESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

The session of the synod was opened on Tuesday in the Bold-st. Chapel. There was a large attendance of ministers. General satisfaction was felt when it was seen that the chairman, the Rev. C. Garrett, was surti- Mewls, recovered from his late illness to preside. The Rev. Owen Watkins was elected secretary, and the Rev. J. T Waddv. 8.A., was appointed assistant secretary. On the calling of the roll, dispensations were granted to the Rev. J. G. Greaves, H. W. Jackson, 8.A., R H. Mole, W. Lisle-Stone, H. S. Sandford, T. M. Budden,and others. The scrutineers appointed were the Revs. T. H. Barrett, W. H. Elug.gins, W. De Tite, and W. George , (convener). The usual inquiries as to character and I ministerial ahilitv were carefully instituted. There were happily no cases of discipline. The only minister who has died within the district dur- ing the year was the Rev. H. M. Radcliffe, of whom an obituary notice was read. Mr. Radcliffe had a useful and peculiarly honoured ministry, and many testified to the beauty of his character. The. Rev. R. Hopkins-Mole becomes' a supernumerary at the coming conference. The Rev. W. Lisle-Stone is also, through illhealth, com- pelled' to retire. Great pleasure was expressed that the Rev. Henry IFlurtost, M A., was able, after three years' retirement, to resume active work. The numerical rehtros were presented. The church membership attinds at 21.983, with 1.372 on trial, and 3,937 junior members. Upwards of 2.000 members are required in this district each rear ti make up for "wear and tear." as repre- sented by the columns " ceased to meet," "deaths," and " emigrations," in the net loss by removals. The dis- trict has not only been et-d. tn.me.ke up this number, but can renort an increase of 107 members. This increase, though net large for so wide an area, is encouraging. inasmuch as it follows upon a very considerable increase last year, and maintains the increase with which the district has been favoured for many years past. The results of the examination of probationers were presented by the Rev. IA il'iarn ()piton. They were of a very satisfactory nature, four having attained to a posi- tion in the honours lists—T. H. Barratt, 8.A., E. W. Lewis, BA., R. E. Brown, 8.A., and H. Martin, M A. On the question of the relation of native ministers t the rea ly :onference, the resolutions sent hie the last conference for the approval of the synods were submitted and accepted with the provision that they should apply to native ministers only. The Rev. T. A. Macdonald brought forward certain resolutions as to t basis of church membership, which became the occa- sion a seriaus debate. It was urged by some that the class meeting should he retained anti carefully gnarded bur that enrolment and attendanee at Holy Communion should he the sole conditions of church membership Rarely has the synod felt so deeply the importance of
any question that it has been called upon to discuss, and the whole temper of the discussion was evidenc,e of this.
OFFICIAL SEMION.

The official sermon was preached at Bewsey-road Church on fuesday evening by the WIT. Justine Hawn, of Liverpool. The text was taken from Jet. xxiii,2B,29. " the prophet that hatli a dream, let him tell a dream, and he that bath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wriest ? saith the Lord. Is not my word like as a fire ? saith the Lord ; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces." In the course of his rem arks the rev. gentleman said despite the most ingenious speculation of man in what were called " the discoveries of modern science," the Bible was able to hold its owo in the world, first of all because of its matchless rasp mse to the undying appeal of tke human soul; an compared with science it was wheat to chaff. Be had no wish to depreciate science. Honour to whom honour was due, and he readily con- ceived that science had laid man under deep thligations, it had invested him with a sort of omnipotence com- pared with the limited pow-re and the kuowledge of his fathers. But where it failed the Bible came in. The Bible responded to man's appeal for relief from the terrors of a guilty conscimce. Science knew nothing about the future life ; it knew nothing about real accountability. What influences and considerations could it bring to bear on a man that would help him in the struggle to be good ? The answer was " None, absolutely none," but " the law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul." &Aimee spoke of the culture of man in his relation to his fellow-man. The Bible went sleeper, on the principle that if they cleansed the fountain the stream would be pure. Thei Bible aimed at character, which underlay culture, and I without it all culture was simply hollow and worthless. But what after death? Science could give no answer absolutely, but where science failed the Bible came in and "life and immortality had been brought to light by the Gospel." Infi ielity never had been popular with men; in the very nature of things it could not be, for just as nature was said to abhor a vacuum, so human nature abhorred negation. An infidel asked a man to I give up his faith in Christ, and the Christian asked, " What will you give me in lieu of all this? I have been in the habit of reading the Binh., and have derived light and comfort from it. What can you give me?" The infidel's creed, if it could he called a creed, was a string of empty negations—no Gad, no Christ, no heaven, no pardan for the guilty, no cleansing for the polluted, no comfort for the bereaved, nu hope of immlrtality for ' the dying. No, no, no—nothing else but "no." It was' a shade worse than trying to feed a hungry man on soap bubbles, but the Bible responded, as science did not, and. could not, to the undying appeals of the human soul. The sermon was followed by the sacrament of the Lord's Supner, to which all the meinty-Ts of the Methodist Church had been invited. During the PIMP evening sermons were preached at various churches in the circuit.

div.head: WEDNESDAYS PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: WEDNESDAYS PROCEEDINGS.

The representative session of the Synod opened on Wednesday. The attendance was very large.—The Rev. J. Binnings moved a resolution expressing the deep sense of the great loss which the whole of Methodism, hut this district especially,had sustained by the death of Edward Ilutchinson,E.q , J.P. The Synod also expressed its heartfelt symp ithy with Mrs. Hutchinson and the bereaved family. It was seeended by Mr. Beckett, J.P. —The resolution was carried, the entire Synod standing and singing two ve.ses of the hymn that formed Mr. Hutchinson'a last message to Mr. Garrett—" Peace, doubting heart, my Grad's I am."—The Synod invited the conference to Liverpool in tbe year 1896. Mr. E. Cannington, J P., was app Anted trustee of the Church Hall, Manchester, in place of Mr. Hutchinson. The fol- lowing elections to conneeinnal committees were made— Home missions, Mr. C. E .yler (Rock Ferry); exten- sion of Methodism, Rev. Owen Watkins and Mr. J. Beckett,J.P. ; educetion,Wee. H. B. Worknian,M.A., and Mr. H. Mathwin, BA. fhe yearly collection shows an increase of over £B, and the general contributions to the Home Mission Fund are fully maintained. Applications were made for the following grants—Carnarvon and Holyhead, £5O each ; Oswestry. £45 ; Welshpool £35 ; Liverpool Mission. £3OO ; flolylake and West lierby,£7o; Tarporley, £3O; Mold £3O; C.rnarvon for Portmsdoc, £3O ; Colwyn Bay for Llanwrst, £3O ; Holyhead and OswestrY. £l5 each ; Gars'ang, £7O; Aberystwith, £6O. The report of the Liverp 'ol Mission was presented by Rev. C. Garrett. The income has been £4.794 12s, 11d., tieing a surplus over expenditure of £s3s. 7d. Preston (Lune-street), not being ready to provide a minister's house, agrees to pay an equivalent of £5O. Temperance affairs were presented be Rev. H. B. Workman, M.A. Thine are 27,667 members of bands of hope, and the adult societies are ahtive. A resolution in favour ot the Local Veto Bill was adopted. The Rev. J. W. Drake was elected the representative to the stationing committee.—ln the absence of Mr. Fishwick Stead, J.P., and Mr. Craze, the affairs of foreign MiS9lins were presentee by R E Strom The district income is £7.309 19; 81. Nearly £3OO had been added by the late Mr. elutellinsnn to meet circuit increases. The average contribution per member in this district is 7s. 61.: that for the entire Connexion is 3s. 51. The following were the representatives to the following con- ference :—Mr. S. M ,sne Rutchineon (109), Mr. W. Ben- nett (Warrington, 98), Mr. Flenshall (Warrington 90), Mr. T. G. Ostiern (Colwyn Bey, 96), Mr. Monkhouse (Liverpool. 81), M. F. J. Norman (Runcorn, 81), Mr. Ef line (Lancaster, 73). Mr. Crsz (Liverpool, 40), Mr. Smith (Whitchurch. 40), and Mr. E. Lewis Lloyd (Liverpool, 40).—Chapel affAirs were presented by the Rev. T. Puddicmr he. The trurt property of the dis- trict is estimated at £902 816 Thanks was given to Mr. M. Standing and Mr. E cardwell for help given in free- ing the Arkholme chapel from debt. Mr. Barber, of Blicknool, has given a minister's house of the value of £l.lOO. The day schools in the district provide for , 13.585 scholars. The Government grant earned is '£20.305 Hs. Id. The Sitn,tav schools have a total of 57,991 scholars, of whom 8 662 are church members. On I the question of the term et ministerial residence in the circuit, Mr. J. Cory Menkhnuse moved the following : —" The rapid increase of the instancesin which the con- ference has been obliged to treat as special cases the ap- pointment of min;srere to mi.s;ons and circuits con- firms the opinion frequ ntly expressed by this synod that steps ought to be taken sin as to modify the eleventh clause of the deed noll as to legalise the appointment of ministers to the use and enj wrnent of trust premises for a longer period than three years, when circumstances rendered such a Course desirable or necessary, and this synod earnestly urges the ennferrens at once to take steps to effect such a modification."—lt was seconded by Mr. J. H. Farmer.—An amendment to the effect that the methods now adopred answer the necessities of the few cases in which a longer residence is desirable was pro- posed by Mr. T. G. o.horn. J.P.,and seconded by Mr. J. Becket, J.P.—The peoposition was carried by a fairly large majority.—A res•lntion calling for prompt punish- ment up..n the authors of the Armenian atrocities was unanimously adopted —A proposal to divide the district at the conference of 1896, brought forward by Mr. Pierce (Wrexham), and seconded by Mr. Osborn, J.P., was carried.

div.head: TRE CLAIMS OF THE YOUNG.
div.p: TRE CLAIMS OF THE YOUNG.
A meeting to Ad v nes te the claims of the young was held in Bewsey-rnui Church nn Wednesday evening. Them was a very fair ftttendacce and the chair was occupied by Mr. E L. Lloyd, nf Liverpool -

- The Rev:J. KtnyLav in introducing the Chairman said that by way of prefer he would like to say a little about the Sunday schonls of the circui,. Including teachers, there were 3,000 coon', noonle in connection with them. There were nearly 2000, in the borough of Warrington, including Sankey Bridges, which was practically part of Warrington, and would soon be in the borough. They , had done their utmost to vet the children and teachers to attend that meeting hut he did not see very many there, and it was very diffi-ult to get young p.ople to meetings during the week. There were, however, many Sunday sehool workers in the R urliPnre, and they must look at the meeting RR bt•inez a very representative one.

_ The CHAIRMAN then addressed the meeting. He said that he was glad to hear Mr. Kirtlan say that that meeting was a repreeentAtion meeting of so large a measure of good, solid work which was being done among the young people gathered in this circuit. That meeting was an experiment, and he was not aware of any Synod where such a meeting WAR being held. He rejoiced greatly that the meeting was being held. He rejoiced greatly that the MQthodiat Church was rousing it,elf in that matter, riser should do their utmost to enlist the sympathies of the young people in the ranks if their church. There were A million scholars in their Sunday schools, and they had it upon the most reliable authority that of this number 80,000 dropped nut, and the question was, what had become of them. He was not going to answer that question, as it was a problem which required to he anlyed by the Sunday schen' workers. He was glad, however, to say that in spite of this dropping out, the numbers attending the schools were increasing. According to the report presented that, afternoon, there were 18,000 Sunday scholars about 15 rears of age, and yet there were only 8,000 attending the society elegy's. They had a right to ask why did not the other 8,000 join the members of the church. They should endeavour to get the co-operation of the officials as well as the ministers of the church. There were a great many mutual improvement societies, Christian Endeavour Societies and like. He had a con- siderable amount of enthusiasm for each of these insti- tutions, hut he claimed that the deepest need of the children, was the spiritual work, and they should try to get the young people more directly connected with the work He had a profound regard for Methodist class meetings—(hear, hear)—and he contended that the Christian Endeavour Society was a class meeting only it was under another name; and the class meeting ought to be made RA attractive as it was possible to make it, and thus attract, the young people to it. _

Th. W.VA.. KIRTIAN said that there was a remarkable society in that circuit, perhapa the most remarkable in the Liverpool district. Daring the last twelve months there was a person in that congregatiPn, who bad gath- ered togeth.r a so-jets- clasa of about 80 young people. He was not certain of the figure which that class contri- buted,hut it was the largest,or almost the largest which was efmtrihil'lll in that circuit. The R ,v.TI F.Kgrxxy then'arldresged the meeti R. lie claimed that the home exercised the greatest I,fluence upon the young people, and a bias was then given to

them which it was almost impossible to counteract in their future life. It was,therefore, absolutely necessary to give a strong character for goodness, to give them a goad start in their home, and this would have a great influence for good in their ~fter life. The Rev. J. W. BuTcaaa urged the ',sung people to adopt the motto of I horough," though not after the fashion of &raty 'rd, who was thorough in badness, but to be thorough for go, dews. He urged them to develop both body, soul and spirit. They should not be afraid of cricket, of football, and of athletics, or anything which would develop the b.)dy to it utmost capacity. They must only remember thatfthe development of the body was a means to am end. They should develop their mind. They should he careful what they read. He did not advise them not to read fiction. He believed that good could be got hype fiction. But let them not read the books which would make them blush to read. Many , books were written in a literary style, and were well re- • viewed in the newsp 5p.411, which were totally unfit to be read. If they had sun b )(As, he advised them to burn : them. That was the very best they could do with them. If they read'fi.;tion don't let them read nothing else as tie was afraid some young piople did. He further urged the young men to be Methodists out and out, and not be afraid ea! being Methodists. They should not expect the church always to do something for them, but rather assist in the church work. Let them keep themselves free from the world unspotted and pure, and make a friend of Jesus Christ, and there would then be no fear for their luure. (Adopiallfe.) The Rev. 0. Bknos said that he was pleased that so much good work was bing done in Warrington among the young. The rev, gentleman then proceeded to give some excellent advice to the children. The rne,•Ung afterwards was brought to a termination in the ugial manner.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
MANCHESTER CORPORA TION AND THE CANAL, COMPANY.
TETE INTEREST ON LOANS.

A meeting of the Soil-) Canal Consultative Committee of the Mauche,iter City Giuncil was held yesterday to consider a report of Mr. Fletcher M tulton, Q.C., as to the best way in which the Corporation can help the Canal Company in nres.int difficulties. It is stated that a sum of £112,500 is due from the Company rto the Corporation in Aucu as half a year's interest on the loan of £5,000,000 made by the Corporation .to the Company. This payment, in addition to £43,000 due as interest far the same period on debentures, would seriously cripple the finances of the Company. Mr. Moulton sug- gests a plan which will give the Company further time for development. The Corporation are in possession of a balance of £llO,OOO, the difference bet- ween the percentage which they pay on the loan of £5,000,000 and the 'oight-r percentage they have charged for it to the company. The recommendation of Mr. Moulton is that the Cnimpary should be required to pay half the interest due in August from the Corporation to the lenders of the £5,000.000—a sum,narnelv.of £40,000, —and that the other h.ll shluld be taken from the pro- fit balance of £llO,OOO. The Committee approved of the suggestion, which will be submitted next Wednee- day to the Manchester City Council. _ . UNLCADING AT LATCHFORD. .

During the week Latchford locks have been a scene of activity, for on Monday the " Monton," a handsome Norwegian boat, irrived at Latchford with 1,200 tons of timber,the biggest part of which is for Mr. It. A Naylor, and a quantity of spruce logs for colliery purposes. The timber for Mr. Naylor, after being unloaded was placed en barges, and in them conveyed to Howley glay. On the same day (Monday), the" John Bull " schooner,with a cargo of cement from L-indon, and consigned to the Warrington Slate Co., Limited, was" berthed" near the Latchford swing-bridge and immediately below the powerful crane which is stationed there, and which hoisted out the cement, some of the latter being placed in the cement store-house close by, and the remainder conveyed direct to the siding at Arpley. Tuesday saw the re-arrival of the " Velinheli," which since last week has been back to Port Dinorwic,and from there brought another cargo of slates for the above-mentioned final. it is interesting to note that this latter boat was unloaded in 6i hours. This speaks well for the docking capaci- ties and facilities at Latchford.

div.head: GEM OF CUE GOLD MINE,
div.p: THE GEM OF CUE GOLD MINE,
LIMITED.

This is a West Australian gold mine, about whose successful future there is no doubt. The Company is distinguished in a way that will commend it to the British investor ; it is the most moderately capitalised West Australian mine hitherto put on the London market. The capital is only £45.000. The mine has been well developed, and reports by the leading Murchi- ' son experts have made on it, all speaking confidently of its prosperous future. Among others, Mr. Norman Whitelaw, late superintendent of pro,p ,cting under the Victorian Government,and Mr. W. Hepburn Gsle,mavor of Cue, from which township the property is only two miles distant, both express themselves in flattering terms regarding the Gem of Cue,the Mayor being so con- fident that he says he regards it as a really good invest- ment. A cable to hand states this the first crushing of 33 tons yielded 45 zi. 12 lwts. The shsres are ss. each, and are being actively dealt in on the London and Pro- vincial Stock Exchanges. They will soon go to a much. higher price than that at which they now stand.

Roberts, Saran Brown, Llovo-at., was charged with assaulting and lo,..atine E num Clayton. 7, Mill-street,on the 7th May.—Mr. Per,y D vie-, appeared for the com- plainant, and s! aced that on Tuesday last about 4.30 the complainant i., ent to bring her clog in as it was fight- ing with defendant's cl• .e, and the defendant threatened complainant with very foul language. Complainant re- monstrated with her and the defendant then picked up a brick and threw it at the complainant, striking her on the ankle. At eight o'clock complainant was in her bowie and defendant climhed on the door and again used very bad language. Complainant,Mr.Davies said, was suffering from heart disease,and was very nervous. —Mra. Clayton gave co. rob rative evidence.—Eliza Bowler, servant ot clmplainant, and Mary Ann Price gave evidence for complainant, and Edward Banner, Mrs. Bellfi -Id, and El zi Atti Pritchard gave evidence for defendant, but it was all so conflicting that the magistra, es di-missed the Ca$AP. ASSAULTS OE THE POLICE.—WINDOW-BREAKING.

At to,- Warrington Pohce Ginn, on Monday morning before Mr. F. Minks and other magi-trates, Michael Murray, 3, Tanner's-lane was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Tanner's-lane on Saturday night ; he was also charged with assaulting P.C. Fish at the same time and place, and also will breaking wilfully and maliciously, two plate glas3 windows, the property of Messrs. W.dk.r and Sons, at the " Three Pigeons," and value £4.—C .nstahlo Fish stated that on Saturday night he was in Winwick-street and near Tanner's-lane, and theie was a large 7,foVoii outside the " Three Pigeons," where the windows were broken. When witness got there the defend.nt was pointed out to him as the perpetrator of the mischief. Murray afterwards rushed at the officer, but the latter took him into custody. Detendant was alm,st naked and as witness was in D dlam-lane he allowed defendant to put his shirt on, and in return the latter butted him with his head. Owing to his breA ng the windows defendant's arm was cut and he was taken to the Infirmary where the wound was dressed.—Mr. Chalmers landlord of the "Three Pigeons," stated that the detendant castle up to him as he was standing at tie door and tried to kick witness who would not let him in. Defendant then lifted up his fiat and hroke the plate-glass window in the door and afterwards broke another with the buckle of his belt.—"lhe bench said that notwithstanding that defendant's arm was badly. cot they could not overlook the assault on the to ilice and he was sent to gaol for 2 months with hard labour. . _

div.head: ALLEGED EMBYZZLMENINT BY A BROTHER.
div.p: ALLEGED EMBYZZLMENINT BY A BROTHER.

At the Warrlinctou Police Court, on Monday, before Me. F. Monks, Aldermen II +l.6s-en and Greeitiall, Messrs. Hayward, William Pierpoinr, and S. Wright. Samuel Pea ce. E•arolie Fearnheiad, was chug d with emii•zzling two sums of money—£2 7s. 81. and £1 51 on the 7th and 20th of March respectively from Herbert Jabez Pearce, his brathsr.—Mr. A. Browne pros-cu-ed, and said that the two Pearces were brothers. Prosecutor was a hosiery manufscturer in BuVerm aket-street, and he had emphi ed his tiro, her to trivel for him :ound the neig,hbotaing country. At the beginning of this year it was discovered that there was something wrong, but it was not found out until about the 6 h of April that de- fendant had received the two sums of money set forth lathe summons from a customer and for which he had not accounte,t. Mr. Brewne's chine. for the sake of the family told defendant that be was not going to prose- cute him. A letter was after wards received from de- fendant expressing his contrition and in which he said that he had taken a house five miles out, and he asked for one more chance as he was starting a new life. He would give up all private ty-uqe cluing and not go the same round that complainant did. Mr. Browne was instructed to write to defendant saying that a warrm.t would not he tiken out against him oil condition that he removed to a distance of 12 miles from prosecutor's shop within seven days, ad not interfere with prose- cutor's business. II defendaiot did not act according to the conditions the prosecutor reserved to himself the right to take out a %arrant against him. Defendant did go away but only to Padgate, and it was found that he had received mi re money of the-irs which he had col- lected. Owing to the relations which existed between the two, and the pleadings of the father, the prosecutor, nevertheless, desired to aek tteir worships that morning to adjourn the summons for three or tour months, and if during that time the defendant withdrew with his family from the district, and promised tit to call upon his brother's customers, the latter woulci then withdraw the summons by permission of the Bench.—The magis- trates granted the adjournment. Defendants were given a chance to improve during the night, hot instead they became worse. It was very Important that order should be kept in such a large establishment, and Mr. Shearer asked that an exainpie might be made of the prisoners. —Miss Lockhart, assistant to the matron, stated that on the day of the , row she went round the wards as usual, and fiend the prisoners taking their food away. On Saturday night between 5 and 7 o'clock he turned up with some money short which he said he had lost. 0. Monday the defendant did not come back with his money and complainant beard that he was under the inn nmee oi drink. A warrant was issued on rhursday morning, but on Saturday the defendant came back and it, turned out that defend int had been on the spre . and had done nothing but drink, and he had assured Mr. Browne that there was nothing wrong whatever. Bis (Mr. Browne's) client after examining the books also found that all was right except as to the defendant getting drunk. Prosecutor did not wish to proceed under the circumstances as it was simply a case of drink. The C4RP was therefore withdrawn. MORS RUFFIANISM —ANOTHER CONSTABLE A,SAULTED

On Tuesday morning betere Mr. IL Garnett (chair- man), Mr. E. J. Guest, and Dr. r. S. Smith, at the Borough Police Court, a charge was preferred against Thomas Brady arid Terence m'Guire for being drunk and disorderly in Town Flll a 11 25 ,in Monday night, also for assaulting Ann Davis at Vie same time and place, and Brady was further charged with assaulting P.C. William Barlow whilst in the exesniti• ri of his duty.— Detective Monaghan stated that at 11 20 on the night in question he was in H rsemarket-s.. in company with P.C. Barlow, and they heard a d.sturbance going on and went to and saw the tel miants kicking at Mrs. Davies' door. They were drunk aid using bad language. Mrs. Davies made a complaint that M'Guire had hit her with a belt. Witnr es took M'Guire into cus- tody,and Barlow took Brady and witness sent assistance to Barlow who was being kicked. Both prisoners were very rough.—P.C. Barlow said that he was with the last witness whose statement was quit- correct. He took , Brady who refused to go and kicked witness on the legs and strark him in the mouth. He behai,ed like a mad- man and witness was rendered valuable assistance by a neighbouring gentleman —Mr. Woodhouse. the gentle- man in question, deposed to seeing Barlow kicked, and he assisted him to bring the man down to the police station.—Ann Davies stated that she was in bed on the night in question and some Men Carae to the door and commenced kicking it. She Came downstairs and heard one say, " Let's make through the window." It was to save the window that she opened the door, and M'Guire struck her on the shoulder with a belt and Brady kcked her. They threatened to tike her life that night and next her husband's, and called her a police spy.—The defendants were each committed for one month's hard labour.

Prosecutor stated that on the night of the Bth May he went to bed leaving 154. in his pockets. His brother William was in the room at the time. Next Morning he got up, put on nis working clothes and went out to work, and at night re- turned, went upstairs for the purpose of putting on the clothes in the pockets of which he had left the money, and found it to be missing. He then gave information to the police.—Patrick Mallett stated that he met William Glynn on the 9th Mliy, and they went to Wigan together to look for work. Prisoner admitted to him that he had taken the money from his brother's clothes. He (Willett) left prisoner on Thursday, and returned home alone.— Prisoner when charged with the theft replied, "Stealing. For the prosecution it was stated that defendant's cat had killed some pigeone,the property of complainant and the latter had sent for defendant to ask him to pay for them. 'MESSES MACMILLAN AND Co.—The fourth of the Illustrated Standard Novels has now been issued in "The Annals ot the Parish" and " Tha Ayrshire Legatees," by John Galt. A very comprehensiie and capable introduction is given by Allred Ainger, who says "The characters and manners of the An- nals of the Parish are those of the reign of George the Third. But they were drawn from life an 1 the narrative loran adopted by the writer required no assistance from plot or intrigue, and the result is that everything in the village history is as fresh, as real, as delightful, as on the day of its appearance.' The chief character in the first story is the Rev Micah Balwhidder, a very curious combination of old-fashionea truth, piety, and wisdom. This per- sonage is not one of whom anyone might take particular notice He has no eccentricities, no peculiarities to distinguish him from a thousand other men in a like position, and yet his personality is so real, life-like, and homely that the reader is unwittingly drawn into an interested perusal, of which for the life of him afterwards he cannot pick out a remarkable feature. The story is full of quaint mannerisms, which to _a 19, h century reader are very amusing, and rendered more so from their wonderful adaptibility and fittingness to the point in hand. The second story is also of much interest —the interest that amuses—and is a chronicle of an unsophisticated family on their travels. By the re-producing of these two narratives a new branch of literature is brought before the present day reader, and one which is worthy of renewed popu- larity, not only for the description of Scottish life which it contains, but for the acute judge of char- acter which the author makes manifest. There are about 400 pages in the volume, and the light, read- able type is printed on antique paper, which, with the faithful illustrations of Mr. Charles E. Brock, harmonises well with the subject of re-production. CASSELL AND CO.—These publishers have earned a world-wide reputation for the excellence of their re-productions of Royal Academy Pictures, and their experiments in that direction have met with gratifying success. Each year there is a series of five magazines containing these pictures, and the first of those for the present year is issue,' this month. The publishers themselves do not hesitate to say that the ,dition of 1895 will surpass in beauty an I perfection any illustrations of a similar nature which have either appeared in their own or any other publication. As most people are aware " Royal Academy Pictures " is a supplement of the "Magazine of Art " and is bound in a similar cover. It is hardly necessary to remark that the printer's art is represented in the highest type of excellence, being remarkable for the distinctness and detail of the engravings. Included in the first number are works by Alma.Tadema. Margaret Dicksee, J. Mac Whirter, P. Graham, R W. Leader, Clayton Adams' Collier, W. F. Yeames, I). Murray, Sadler, Wyllie, Henrietta Rae, and a num- ber of others, all of whom are represented by a sample of their work almost equal to the original. —The May number of the " Magazine of Art " is of extraordinary interest. The frontispiece is aphoto- gravure reproduction of Sir F. Leighton's "Greek Girls Playing at Ball." The second plate is an etch- ing of Monsieur Bail's picture "After the Day's Work"; and in addition to these there are a factimile reproduction of a study by Mr. F Dicksee, I t A., and a full-page wood engraving of M. Barrau's " The Way of the Cross. Catalonia." The contents include Mr. M. H. Spielmann's preliminary notice of the Royal Academy; an important article by Mr. Lionel Oust on the " Portraits of J M. W. Turner, R.A.." fully illustrated; a paper on " M. Hellen s Dry-Points," by Mr.!. Wedmore. Mr. Alexander Ansted writes upon "The Cathedral Closes of Salis- bury and Wells." illustrating his article himself. " An American Landscape Painter," by Mr. W. H. Downes, deals with the work of Mr. Mark Water- man, and there is an article on " The Mosaics of Sir Ed ward Burne-Jones." Mr. Rupert Bunny supplies a charming design to one of Herrick's poems.. The number concludes with the usual illustrated " Chronicle of Art."

GEORGE NEWNES AND CO.—ln common with " Round the World," these publishers have issued the first of a series of books illustrating the points of interest on the sea-board of Great Britain and Ireland under the title of "Round the Coast." This ' edition is in all respects similar to its predecessor, and during the holiday season should possess spec- ial attraction to all the pleasure-seekers in the 1 klngdom. 1 here are 24 beautifully printed pictures in each parr,the price is 6d. only. CHAPMAN AND HALL,LIMITED.—The dense ranks of sixpenny magazines ot fiction have been swelled by one more representative in the tastefully pre- pared " Chapman's Magazine," edited by Oswald Crawfurd. The contents for the first number are as follows :—" In the Hollow of the Hills," serial story by Bret Harts ; "Bad Matches," Anthony Hope ; " For the Cause," Stanley J. Weyman ; "The Experi- ence of Inspector Barrie," by George Ira. Brett ; " A Noiseless Burglar," by James Payn; " Reggie's Rival," Frankfort Moore; " A Hard iN oman,' serial by Violet Hunt ; "An age-end ballad of a poet born," by John Davidson, Both , serials, though intensely opposite in theme and character appear likely to develop into narratives of peculiar interest as they proceed ; indeed the open- ing chapters impel a desire for an early and rapid continuation of the story. " The Experiences of Inspector f3ttle," of the Criminal InvPstigation department are detective stories of the firs, water. A start is made in "The murder at .fex farm" out of which the detective unravels with wonderful faci- lity a clue which promises well. Deductive, and "putting two and two togather " powers of the highest order are evinced,and this type of literature will have a valuable augmentation on the comple- tion of this series. All the short. stores are full of novel conceptions and are' productive .of a large amount of interesr,while one or two are written as dialogue or as a drama, (witness " F.lr the Cause,") but their attraction is no less diminished.

T. FISHER UNwiN.—The special feature of the May number of the " Century Magazine " is the illustrated article on the discovery of the tree at the foot of which the heart of Dr.. Livingstone wss buried on May 411 1873. Mr. F. J. fllave, working in the interest of the " Century " discovered the tree which is the largest in the neighbourhood. On it is an inscription cut by a devoted servant of the great missionary. There are illustrations showing the tree and its discoverer, and the narrative itself is interesting as publishing " the te,itimonv of the camera to the preservation during 29 years of the one landmark in " Dark,Ast Africa " that has inter- est for the entire civilize I world." All the other contents of the magaz'ne are equal to the rezuhir standard of excellence which the " Century " has a mane for.

DR. TANNER AND MAJOR JONES.
A FIERY CORRESPONDENCE,

The following 1.4 the latest and most complete version of the correspon&nce between Dr. Tanner and a Major Jones, of Pr zaace, who wanted to give him " satisfac- tion " Dr. Tanner received the fcllowing telegram from M4jor J nes, of Penzlnce at the House of Commons on Monday :—" In rel-ly to your despicable question about the Duke of Cambridge I designate you a coward. De- lighted to give you Sati4action across the water ; pis- tols." To this th N Ltionalist Whip replied :—" Wire received. Will meet you to-morrow in Constantinople, under the Tower of Gralati,midnight. Being challengt d, preler torpedoes. Bring another ass.—TANNER." Ano- ther despatch from the Cornish watering-place was de- livered at Westmioister :—" Unwittingly you have con- firmed my t legratn, but not the challenge.—J. JONES, major." Dr. Tanner's second message raa thus :—" The fourth wire—Sorry you funked the torpedoes. Stick to Con.tantinoole, bring the inoke. -TANNER." There the fiery correspondesce remains for the present.

div.p: SHIP CANAL.
ARRIVAL OF AN ANCHOR LINER.

- On Wednesday morning, the steamer Nubia entered the canal from Glasgow, where she had been receiving a portion of her cargo, for Manchester, where she will receive cargo for Bombay, Kurrachee, and the Indian coast ports. She is one of the fleet of the Anchor line, and is the longest steamship that has yet navigated the waterwar, her len.,th between perpendiculars tgeing 378 feet, or 8 feet longer than the ICtisow, of the China Mutual line, which had hitherto hell the record. The Nubia is commanded by Captain Knox, and her gross register is 3.551 tons, her carrying capacity exceeding 5.0:0 tons. The Clan Ranald, tithe Clan line,is now at tilasgow, and is expected to arrive in 4 anchester in the course of a few days, to load for India. The Oopack, a steamer of 3,883 tons gross register, the property of the China Mutwil steam Nav;gation Company, is now on passage from Glasgow. for Manchester, where she will receive cargo for Penang, Singapore, Hong Kong, Shanghai, and the principd ports in Japan THE ERECTION OF WAREHOUSES. _ . .

A cmpany has been -Tort-tied with £lOO,OOO capital (already subscribed) for the construction, under an ar- rangement with the Ship Canal Company, of a series of large warehouses at the Salford docks. The contracts will probably be let before the end of the present month. This essential part of the canal equipment will therefore he completed without the neceasity of any further appli- cation to PArliament for borrowing powers. There are to be seven fire-proof warehouses, each of four storeys, on the south side of No. 6 Dock, tor grain and general merchandise, and thirteen seven-storey warehouses, specially designed for the storage of cotton, on the north side of No. 8 Dock.

div.head: LATCHFORD LOCK QUESTION.
div.p: THE LATCHFORD LOCK QUESTION.

The steamer Harold, which was concerned in the un- fortunate accident at Latchford on the 10th April, was towed out of the canal by two tugs on Satuiday after- noon, after havine been detained by the canal authori- ties for over a month. She waa taken to Birkenhead and placed in the Clover Graving Dock, where she is now undergoing repairs.
