div.head: OUR LOCAL CEURCBES-WARRINGTON
div.p: OUR LOCAL CEURCBES-WARRINGTON
WYCLIFFE P.S..A.

The meeting of Sunday was presided over by the Rev. John Yonge (president),who in the course of his address referred to the character of Nehemiah in one especial particular as worthy of imitation, viz., his power in re- fusing to do what he knew to be wrong. He was a man who knew how to say " No." The speaker for the after- noon was Mr D. Shilton Collin, of Liverpool, who de- livered an exceedingly able and thoughtful address upon " The way in which men shape their destiny," his sub- ject being the words of Paul in Acts xvii., " And the times of this ignorance God winked at. Be now corn- maid .th all men everywhere to repent: because Be hath appointed a day in which He will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom He bath ordained." The solo, was sung by Mr. Jones, a member of the P.S.A., and the lesson was read by Mr. B Foreman, prayer being offered by Mr. George Ba 3 ley. Owing to the volunteer funeral the at- tendance was not so large as usual. It may be men- tioned that next Sunday is the open Sunday afternoon when the speaker will be Mr. F. H. Smith, J.P., of Swinton, Manchester. PADGATE WESLEYAN CHURCH.

On SunCl;7,Thse-ar;rirv-e;;;;Y—se;Y-iWri-ii;-connection with the at;(.ve place of worship were held morning, after') )on, aid evening, when there were very good congregations despite the rather threatening weather. The preacher in the morning and evening was the Rev. George Hammond, of Manchester, and his discourses were listened to with rapt attention. His morning subject was upon the subject of temptation, and his evening subject was "genuine conversion." During the morning service the choir sang the anthem, "If ye love Me," and "Calvary " was sung at the evening ser- vice,Miss M. Bennett tastefully taking the solo part. In the afternoon a flower service was held, Miss Bessie Dutton presiding,and during the course of the af ternovn she gave a very interesting address. The flowers were afterwards given to the Warrington Infirmary. During the day special hymns were sung,the choir and children being under the leadership of Mr. James Bennett. of Bewsey. Miss J. Bennett, of Lyndhurst, officiated as organist. The collections for the day realised £22. BANK QUAY MISSION.

The Sunday school anniversary services in connection with the Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay, were held on Sunday, when the preacher in the morning and evening was the Rev. W. G. Thompson, of Didsbury College. There were good congregations at each service and also in the afternoon when a sacred service of song entitled "Rescued in Londm " was rendered by the choir and children. The children looked extremely well, for they were all dressed in white, and thus added to the appearance of the beautiful chapel. The connective readings were given by Mr. 11. M. Ashton, assisted by Mr. Joseph Monks, junr. Messrs. J. Baker, and S. Millington took the solo parts, and the quartette party consisted of Mrs. J. Monks jour., Miss Ashley, Messrs. S. Hassell and S. Millington. The choir and children were under charge of Mr. J. Mills, and Mr. F. Atkinson presided at the organ, and much credit is due to these gentlemen for the manner in which they had trained them. The collections for the day amounted to £633.4d.

div.head: LY1431.
div.p: URBAN COUNCIL.—The monthly meeting of this authority was held on Tuesday night, in the Council's offices, under the presidency of Air. James Gregson. There were also present—Messrs. Welford (vice-chair- man), Bolt, Mclntyre, Brown, Gould, and Smith, with Mr. Ridgway (law clerk), and Mr. W. Mullard (secre- tor( ).—The Law Clerk produced a letter, written by Mr. Charles Lon shaw, calling the Council's attention to what he considerod ta be encroachments upon the public highway by the erection of a wall in front of a hedge in Statham-lane, and also one opposite the Plough Hotel. He added that he had spoken to the Survey.,r about the matter, but that as that gentleman could give him no satisfactory reply, he had determined to lay it before the Council.—Mr. Smith proposed,and Mr. Gould seconded, that the letter be referred to the Roads Com- mittee to report upon.—The motion was then carried.- -Mr. Smith said he had ascertained that meeting on the second Tuesday in the month for the transaction of the Council's business was rather unsuitable to the members and that the majority, if not all of them, preferred the first Friday in the month. He, therefore. begged to move that the monthly meetings of the Council be in future held at seven o'clock on the first Friday in each month, and that the resolution passed at the annual meeting fixing the meeting day on the second Tuesday evening le rescinded.—Mr. Brown seconded, and the proposition was carried.—The Law Clerk was instructed to write to the LOCRI Government Board asking them if the applica- tion of the Lymm Urban District Council for the powers and duties of a Parish Opuncil relative to the appoint- ment of overseers and the revocation of appointment of assistant overseer, had yet been considered.—Replying to Mr. Welford, the Law Clerk said that "the powers and duties of a Parish Council" would include the Coun- cil's adtrenistration of any charity,otherwise than eccle- siastical. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.—Tho Sunday school sermons in connection with the Lymm Primitive Met hodist Chapel were held on Sunday afternoon and eyvnitig. Mr. Robert Robinson, of Manchester. wa the preacher. The congregations were large, and the collections, which were taken in aid of the Sunday school, were liberal. ELECTION OF A GUARDIAN.—The election to fill the vacancy in the representation of Lymm district upon the Bucklow Union of the Poor Law Guardians, created through the resignation of the Rev. G. W. Guest, M.A., rector of Lymm, took place on Saturday. Polling boDths were situated in each of the four wards—Lymm, Bboth's Hill, Reatley, and Statham—at which the recording of votes was made somewhat slowly. The candicirtes were Mr. J. R. Smith, fustian manufacturer and mer- chant, of Manchester, residing at Birch Brook Lodge, Heatley ; and Mr. John Wilkinson, of Platt Farm, Hestley, the former gentleman being the nominee of the Conservatives, and the latter gentleman of the Liberals. The result was :—Smith (C), 307 ; Wilkinson (L), 296 ; majority for the Conservatives 11 votes. Mr. Smith,the successful candidate, was formerly a member of the Manchester Board of Guardians.

div.head: STOCKTUR HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTUR HEATH.

THE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.— A. meeting of the Apple- I ton Parochial Committee was held at the London Bridge Inn, Stockton Heath, on Frichy. Mr. , Josepla Knowles occupied the chair, and there were also present : Messrs. C. :W. Davenport, .J. Whitlow, Pearson, Coppock, J. Darbyshire, Hamnson, Farrington (inspector), and J. Ashton (clerk). It was resolved on the motion of Mr. Davenport, secanded by Mr. Whitlow, that Mr. Knowles be appointed chairman of the committee. Mr. Henry Eyes was appointed vice-chairman en the motion of Mr. Whitlow, seconded by Mr. Davenport. In accordance with instructions the Clerk reported that he had written to the trustees of the Duke of Bridgewater, and Mr. Barry called upon him and stated that the trustees hoped the committee would not at present insist upon the exe- Cu tion of the works in Cawdor-at. and Bedford-st., and I the streets abutting, and also Northwich-road, se as to enable the District Council to take over the streets as highways, it was resolved that the further considera- tion of the matter be deferred. It was also decided that the Corporation of Warrington be requested to fix and maintain proper fire plugs at convenient distances, and that Messrs. Davenport, Whitlow, Cuppock, Hampson and Pearson tie appointed a committee to determine the places where the plugs should be fixed.—The minutes were ri ad at the meeting of the Runcorn Rural Council on Tursdav afternoon and were approved of en the motion of Mr. Efeywood, seconded by Mr. Brandreth. A NINIVERSARY Seavicks,—The Sunday school anniver- sary services, in connection with the Ebenezer Wesleyan Church, weir: held on Sunday. Mr. Allen, of Lymm, preached in the morning and afternoon, the Rev. J. S. Hughes, fiap'ist minister, of Hill Cliff, in the evening,to a large congregation, from the words, "Thanks be unto God for His unspeakable gift." Musical selections were given by an augmented choir, and all the services were much enjoyed.

John James Mago, a quiet, middle-aged man, has had a career as romantic as that tof Monte Cristo. Mago is now a Guatemalan millionaire, who lives nine months out of the year in Paris. Twenty years ago be was a poor English collector of insects in Guatemala, and also acted as the British Vice-Consul at San Jose.

One day Commandante Gonzalez ordered Mago to appear before him. Mago sent word that he would come in a short time. This incensed the Commandante, and he sent a file of soldiers after Mago, and, when the in- sect collector appeared, order seventy•five lashes to be laid upon his bare back. This was done very thoroughly and when it was finished, Gonzalez shouted . " Give him twenty-five metre for luck." When Mago recovered, which was only after careful nursing, as his back was badly cut up,he made a formal complaint to the British Government. The result was that Guatemala was ordered to punish Gonzalez, and to pay Mago one hundred pounds for every lash he had re- ceived. In default of this English cruisers would shell San Jose and other coast cities.

Guatemala readily punished Gonzilez, but tried hard to evade paying ten thousand pounds to Miter). The British however, were inexorable, and the poor collector was made a comparatively rich man in one day. A 4 he had more doin than anyone in the country at that time. President Barrios went into partnerbhip with him.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR ON THE L. &N.-W. RAILWAY.
div.p: MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR ON THE L. &N.-W. RAILWAY.
A BODY FOUND IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE.

An inquest was held at the Police Court on Friday, by Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner,upon the body of a male child whicn was found in a third-class compartment of a railway train early yesterday morning. Mr. Fenna, solicitor, was present on behalf .of the Lond,no and North-Western Railway Co. Joseph Birchall, 50, Nicholson-st., a guard in the employ of the L. & N.-W.R. Co. said that he was going as a passenger from Wigan to Warrington in the train which left Wigan at 2.41. No one was in the compartment but himself. He put his lamp on the floor, and the light shone upon a bundle under the seat. He picked up the bundle and saw it bore the address pr.duc- ed. (The Coroner said that it was not advisable that the address should be at present disclosed as the police were making inquiries). Socn after leaving Wigan he opened the parcel and found it contained toe body of a child which was covered with a chemise, newspaper, brown paper, and red wrapping. The newspaper was an Aber- deen paper, and the train had come from Aberdeen. tie gave information on arriving at Warringt-n to the sta- tion master, the guard and police. He got to Warrington at 3.2 a.m. The door was not open when he went to the train at Wigan. Dr. T. Starkey Smith said that he had examined the body at his house. On unwrapping the parcel, he found it was a full grown male child which had not been pro- perly attended at birth. There were no marks of vio- lence upon the body. He made a post-mortem examina- tion at the police station and was of opinion that the child had breathed. The lungs were fully inflated and when removed they floated in water. He could not,how- ever, positively say whether the child had had a separate existence. The stomach was empty, but the organs were perfectly healthy. The child had not been washed nor had it been attended to in any way.—By Inspector Spinks : He thought the child was born on Thursday. The Coroner said that alter the doctor's evidence, he could only direct the jury to find that the child was still born. By law, unless it was conclusively proved that the child had a separate existence, it must be assumed that the child was still born. Dr. Smith was unable to prove that there had been a separate exist- ence, and though some person might be respans;ble for concealment of birth or some other offence,with that the jury had nothing to do. Mr. Fenna said that the railway company did all they could to endeavour to find out the passengers who had travelled in that compartment, and information was sent to Liverpool where a man who was supposed to have travelled in that compartment was stopped and his name and address had been taken. The Company were doing everything in their power to assist the police. The jury returned a verdict that the child was still born.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL NOTES.
div.p: TOWN COUNCIL NOTES.

Warrington's local Parliament opened its sitting in a loose and languid style on Tuesday evening week. There was, to begin with, only a moderate attend- ance of members, and indeed the appearance of the Council Chamber a minute or two before the Mayor took the chair was scarcely promising of even a quorum. The flue weather out-of-doors evidently had its attractions even for town councillors. But within a few minutes of the opening of the busi- ness, members trooped in until the Chamber had something like its normal appearance on a Council night. For a time the procee iings were conducted with remarkable expedition, and after the Mayor had briefly alluded to the death of Mr Joseph Tay- lor, a former member of the C iuncil, the minutes of no fewer than ten of the committees were passed without discussion. The only break in the formal moving and seconding of the,4e minutes was when Councillor Roberts on behalf of the Museum Com- mittee acknpwledged the varions gilts of specimens of British shells, and other objects, made to the museum by Mr. fleathcote, the expert who is re-ar- ranging the shell collection at the museum. The specimen spresented were, Mr. Roberts said, very valuable ones, andwould help to mike the Warring- ton collection one of the bet in the North of Eng- land.

The real business of the evening began as soon as the Markets Committee laid before the Council its recommendation to transfer the pig market to the old Militia Barracks. Alderman Greensll, who, by the way, was again in attendance after a rat her long absence, was the proposer of the minutes, and Alderman Blackhurst the seconder. The latter gentleman asked the Town Clerk to read a communication from the Board of Agriculture on the subject. This document stated that an in- spector of the Board had heed to Warrington and had come to the conclusion that the present matket arrangements were "quite unworthy of such an influential town as Warrington, and that the Barracks were much superior for the pur- poses of a cattle market to the Fair Ground. Alderman Wright at once commenced to voice the opposition to the project, and moved that the pro- posal of the committ te be rejected. He also read a memorial signed by 110 " very important and very large ratepayers," asking the Coun-il to wiih!iold its consent to the scheme as it would " not only be detrimental to the health of the dis•-rict inu, dis- astrous in its consequences to the property. of the neighbourhood in causing tenants to leave the dis- trict." Some objection wHA made to the reading of this memorial but the Mayor ruled that it was in order, and as some of the councillors declared that they must have" all or none " of the names,Alderman Wright went though the whole list. The amendment was seconded by ' Alderman Francomh whose principal argument seemed to be that while there had never been an epidemic at Town Hill, the swine market would be , a cause of unhealthiness at tne Barracks, because lof the defective sewerage at the hitter place. Like I Alderman Wright tie declared in favour of the vacant ground in Queen-street as a I more suitable site for the market, Alderman Hutchinson, although a member of the Markets Committee, went against his colleagues on this subject. He was in favour of taking the pigs to Longford as they would then have all the smells together, a reference to that odoriferous locality which caused some loughler. Councillor Roberts was decidedly of opinion that if the pig market was not fit for Wilson Patten-mt. it was not fit for Town Hill, but be was not convinced that the best possible site had yet been tound. He therefore suggested that the subj.ct should be further con- sidered by the two Committees concerned—the Markets and the Heath (if 1111 mit-tett—who could also take into account the cpiesrioos of it cattle market and a public abattoir. Councillor Shaw and Coun- cillor Smethurst supported the amendment, Coun- cillor Shaw Green supported Councillor Robert's suggestion, while Councillor Monk.; and Councillor Woods both supported the committee. The amend- ment was then voted upon and was rejected by 12 votes to 11. This, however, did not save the com- mittee's proposal as Couocillor Roberts in order to have his previous suggestion acted upon, proposed a second amendment, providing for the closing of the market on Town Hill, hut leaving out the pro- posal to take it to the LS irraoks. This amendment was carried by sixteen votes to six.

The most important hu,leess now left to be dealt with was the Dropoal of the Gas Committee to borrow £20,000 to meet the cot of closing the Mersey-street gas works. It wa4 pointed out by the Chairman of the Gas Committee, Councillor T. Fairclough, that gas is at preQent manufactured in Mersey-street at al, and that therefore the concentration of the whole of the gas works at Longford would be a saving to the Corporation. In the debate which foil wed Councillor Roberts strongly urged the cbtims of gas consumers to a reduction of price but in the end the Committees proposal was adopted.

Sir.--Will you allow me through your • colums to ex- press my sincere thanks to Mr. Ohniy for the use of his Circus on Thursday night last for my benefit and also to the Mayor and Mayoress and other ladies and gentlemen who so warmly supported me on my benefit night. VHE NEWTON DISTRICT PUBLIC ELEMEN- TARY EDUCATION CO M. 111 ITT KE. should like to know how the Executive of the above committee is constituted. I understood, on its formation, that it was to consist of (1) a representative from the various schools ; (2) a ratepayer's representa- tive for Newton, Wargrave and Earlestown ; (3) three Commissioners' representatives ; but from what Jean gather this arrangement has not been adhered to—or I am wrongly isformed. Perhaps one of the ratepayers' 07 Commissioners' represematives will ascertain at the next meeting of the Committee whether the following are facts or not. (a) Did Mr. Ormand act last year in the dual capacity of Chairman of the Executive Com- mittee and manager of the Wesleyan School ? (b) Is not Mr. Gooding who acts as secretary to the committee also a manager and correspondent of the WesleYan school ? (c) Is it not also a fact that J. W. Emmet, Esq., J.P., is manager of the Wesleyan school ? lithe above ques- ions are answered in the affirmative then it fellows that the Wesleyan school has three representa- tives to the Executive Committee. Wargrave and the Vulcan infant school (to all intents and purposes one sghooll are represented by Messrs. Borron and Carson, whilst Newton school is represented by D. Watkin, who sets as the chairman of the General Committee, and who, therefore has. on critical divisions two votes. The Earlestown District School,the next to the largest school, if not the largest, has but one representative. I am one of a large number that think this a most unfair arrangement, and especially when one considers what advantage has been taken of it. With your permission I intend to refer to the sot jsct again. I can only hope that, as fresh Commissioners' representatives have been appointed, the committee will be reorganised,and that a Limited number of school managers (say,in proportion to the average attendance of the schools—the actual num- ber being settled at the end of each school year) will be appointed to act on both the General and Executive Committees.—Thanking you in anti,iustion of the insertionof this letter,—I am, yours truly, RATEPAYER.
Earleatown, May 15th.

PEACE AT ANY PRICE. "Think not that ' am come to sen i peace on earth : I etuste not to send peace. but. a sword."—Matt. x. 34. Sir,—l think it high time someone showed the other aide of the twaddle which has lately been running through your columns on the subject of Peace. Now, peace is doubtless a priceless lan.,n, if righteously ob- tained and maintained; but is much too dearly bought by the sacrifice of honour or at the price of national de- gradation. There is a certain section of pietistic cranks among U 8 who dream of peace between nations, who, intetit.upou one interpretation of certain passages of the Christian mythology would have England disarm in face of armtd Eur•ope. Now whatever value the mischievous dogmas of this mythical personage may have for per- sonal application, nations have not yet got to the height of absurdity involved in turning the other cheek to the amiter, or "taking no thought for the morrow " in the shape of pretiaration to resist aggression. What these "goody goody " folks should do is to preach their pecu- liar doctrines to the European dogs of war, now strain- 1 ing at the leash, impatient to be slipt. As an example of the inanities into which people can drift upon this subject—take the late utterances of the lady who asks "is war a necessary evil?" a fitting answer to this question is, "'That depends—upon cir- cumstances." Thus, let any of the "Great Powers" of Europe become thoroughly convinced that England had inally and unchangeably adopted the doctrine of non- resistance to aggression, and the "Secietv of Friends" would quickly lose the platform from which they preach this "peculiar doctrine." It is only by virtue of the fact that England is armed and ready for the fight, that Miss Ellen Robinson is enabled to preach against armaments. This lady also speaks of the military training of some Sunday school children, and deprecates " this training of children before they were old enough to think for themselves." Now really,Miss Robinson,l beg of you to think a little for yourself! In this you have aimed a deadly blow at all Sunday school teaching; for what chance would her" peculiar doctrine" have if people 11,1 learned to" think for themselves" ere the attempt was made to teach them*? Fortunately for her views this faculty of " thinking for themselves " is a very rare one! —Yours truly.

div.head: PRO ARIS ET FOCIS.
div.p: PRO ARIS ET FOCIS.
THE ARMENIAN ATROCITIES.

Sir,—"Aßeader" seems to have taken umbrage at my previous remarks upon the above, hut he effers no argu- ments to prove that they were wrong. A silly question and a little lauding of the pastor of W 5 cliffe are sorry methods of dealing with a profoundly interesting sub- ject. Your correspondent tells us that the 'sermon in question was delivered " before a living and admiring congregation." Of course it was. I never imagined that Mr. Yonge would preach to dead men ; and the matter and tone of his discourse were admirably suited to the palate of his hearers. Rut has" A Reader " for- gotten the Scripture which says " What is highly esteemed among men is abominatlon in the sight of God." For my own part, 1 seldom see or hear of a crowd gathering round some popular preacher without being reminded of the Lord's solemn warning to his disciples," Woe unto you when all men speak well of you, for so did their fathers to the false prophets." Fer- sezution, and not popularity, ever was,and ever will be, the lot of,the preachers of the Christianity of Christ. If Mr. Yonge and his people were believers in Islamism I should, of course, expect their faith to be leavened with the sanguinary spirit of the Koran. As they are not Mohammedans, however, but pose some- what prominently as followers of the meek and lowly rrinee of Peace I was surely entitled to regard their sermon and memorial as rather antagonistic tb the tender, loving and forgiving life and teaching of the Master whom ;hey profess to serve. A careful and I trust, honest reading of the New Tes- tament led me long ago to the conclusion that war, under any circumstances whatever,was simply human savagery inspired and fanned by the powers of darkness ; and a gross violation of the letter and spirit of the gospel of peace and goodwill to men. If this view is correct,hew saddening and discouraging it is,Mr. Editor, to find men sitting in our churches and chapels, under *hat they are pleased to call a Christian Ministry,who are not ashamed to avow their adhesion to the policy of the sword in set- tling disputes! But when a statesman declarea war against some distant nation, ChriAtian or pagan, and the drum beats to arms,how coward ly,how contemptible is the conduct of the apologists of fiehting ! Instead of rushing to the front of the battle,as one would naturally suppose they would do, tn prove their devotion to their principles by rifle and bayonet ; battalions of wretched men, drawn from the lower ranks of poverty and hired for a few coppers a day, are sent out to do the murdering ; while they remain at home and enjoy the nelvspaper reports of the carnage as it goes on from time to time / Sir, if I could bring myself to believe that the Chris- tianity of Christ lent its sanction in any way to the horrible atrocities of the battle fle!d. I should cease to regard it as a Divine institution. and look upon it an mereiy a human religion destined to pass away in its tirts.—Yours truly,

div.head: THB WHIT-MONDAY DEMONSTRATIONS.
div.p: THB WHIT-MONDAY DEMONSTRATIONS.

Another Meeting ot the Committee who are organising the above demonstration of the Sunday schools', was held in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom on Friday evening last week. The business to be transacted was the draw, for posi- tions in the procession, wnich resulted in the Primitive Methodists getting first place, Brunswick Wesleyans second, Baptists third, Vulcan Wesleyan fourth, Salvation Army fifth, Wel-h last. The bands engaged are Earlestown and nutr.on Road. EARLESTOWN ESLEYIN Z.,IINDAY SCHOOL. The anniversary services in aid of the funds of the above school were held in the Wesleyan Chapel ,on Sunday. The day was rather against large con- gregations, but in spite of this the chapel was crowded on each occasion. The services were con- ducted morning and evening by the RAC'. RA. Mitcheson Brown of Manchester, who preached practical and instructive sermons. The ordinary show was augmented by a large choir of girls, who assisted in the musical portions of the service, in the evening Miss L. Barr, and Miss E. Collinge sing- ing solos in excellent taate. In the afternoon, a sacred contata, "Two Seasons," was given by the children and choir. The various solos were sung by Misses M. Clare. A. Eckersley, Higgins, L. Barr, C. Berry, E. Collinge, M. Roberts, L. Monks, Messrs.l F. P. Clare, J. Sudwortli, and J. R. Barr. The accompaniments were played by the Earlestown Orchestral Society, under the leadership of Mr. F. Whatmough, aryl Miss E. L. Greenall, organist, Mr. Clare officiating as conductor. In the evening at the close of the service, the choir sang the Halle- lujah chorus. The collections during the day amounted to £57. GOOD TEMPLARY AT EADLESTOWN. . .

On Monday evening the hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Templars held their weekly meeting in the Co-operative Hall. At 7 o'clock the juveniles ' met, and were presided over by Bro. E. Newman, D.S.J.T. There was a good number of membsrs and adults present. The temple was visited by Bro. A. Newell, D.C. Sec., of Liverpool, who gave a most earnest and interesting address, taking for his sub- ject" The child; what will he b-come," illustrated by a series of appropriate pictures. Sister A. New- man sang a solo "I am waiting." At 8.30 the juvenile temple was formally closed, and the adult lodge was opened under the presidency of Bro. W. Wilson, C.T. The digest of business for the district lodge was read by Bro. E. Newman, L.D., who also gave a report of No. 1 Convention held on Saturday. Bro. A. Newell was then introduced to the lodge with the usual honours, after which he presented an illuminated emblem of the order to Bro. Hopkins for having been the means of induc- ing the largest number of new members to join tie lodge during the quarter. the emblem being the present of Bro. J. B. Holliday, treasurer. Bro. Hopkins responded, and said he worked for the emblem not so much with the object of gaining a prize as to show a good example to his own boys and to those with whom he came in contact. He expressed a hope that, the presentation of the emblem would be an inspiration and encourage- ment to the younger members of the lodge to per- severe and work for the order on all occasions. Bro. Newell gave a very earnest address to the members, referring to the work of the Good Templar Order generally, and the need at the present time for earnestness, to arouse public opinion on the Veto Bill now before Parliament. Thanks were accorded to Bro. Newell for his visit and address, and on the motion of Bro. J. Halton it was arranged to hold an open meeting next session, Bro. Clarke being re- sponsible for the programme.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
(BY AN OCCASIONAL CONTRIBUTOIL)

Now that the great festival of the year is safely over we can do with a drop of rain. We had a slight downfall on Sunday, but it hardly laid the dust. Since then we have had a strong wind blow- ing from the North West, which has quickly dried the roads, and at the ptesent time is blowing the dust in clouds much to the inconvenience of pedestrians and reminding one of a boisterous day in March. The fields present a hard dry appear- ance,and the farmers are beginning to take a serious view of the situation. Rain is badly wanted for the growing crops, and unless it comes speedily, 11 the damage will be incalculable.

All Earlestown, and crowds of people from other places, turned out to witness what has now become the most important public event of the year in Earlestown. Without a doubt the show was a good one, and if it improves in the next few years, as it has done since its inception, Earlestown will not be large enough to hold the large number of visitors, who will be certain to put in an appearance. It is pleasing to notice the interest the townspeople take in the affair, but I certainly think the trades- men, who are by far the greatest gainers, might patronise it a little more. There was not very I much to complain of in the matter of decoration, but even in this more enthusiasm might be shown, and perhaps the hint will not do any harm for future occasions.

The scene on the marshalling field was one to be remembered with pleasure, for the gathering was one of real brilliancy, the mixing of the colours being most charming. The task of marshalling the something like 2,500 children, was one that I would not care to undertake, still, I think the manner in whicti it was carried out, could be improveil upon. A programme, showing the order of the procession, had been issued. but it became hopelessly mixed, and it was imposAbie to follow the procession with the programme. Again, when leaving the field no kind of order was kept, many of the children having to run to keep up anything like a connec- tion. It would be well in future to allot certain places in the field for the different characters, and as they arrive it should be theduty of the marshals to see that the characters proceed to their allotted places, and with the aid ot several assistants, the marshals should see that no departure was made. The assistance should also be obtained in keeping the procession in something like order, as children have a peculiar habit of rambling all over the place, if not restrained.

Now, a word as to. the judging of the turnotits. No conditions for comoetition are issued by the committee, a circular simply being issued to the effect that prizes of a certain value will be given for the cleanest and best turnouts. Many of the tradesmen competed for the prizes, and there is not the slightest doubt the carters had gone to con- siderable trouble to make their horses and vans clean and respectable, and upon this they ex- pected to be judged. They were disagreeably sur- prised however after the judges had inspected the horses and vans, when they were ordered to trot round. The men took it that the competition was upon the appearance of their horses, and not upon their action, and consequently there was much grumbling. I perfectly agree with the men, and consider it was not fair to the men to judge as to the action of their horses. In future it would be well if the May Queen Committee increased the nrize money, and charge an entrance fee to compe- , titors, and at the same time issue conditions, so that men may know upon what grounds they are competing.

div.head: VIE EXAMINER -SATURDAY, MAY 18. 1895
div.p: VIE EXAMINER -SATURDAY, MAY 18. 1895
A. RUNCORN DISTRICT COUNCILLoR IN THE BANKRUPTCY COURT.

At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court yesterday,before Mr. Registrar Nicholson, William Martin Williams, 8 Leinster-st., late of Bridgewater Arms lime], Gilbert-st., Runcorn, licensed victualler, underwent his public ex- ination. The examination was conducted by Mr. A. B. • Potter, the assistant official receiver. The gross liabili- ties were £353105. Id., and the assets were nil. The bankrupt stated that he was a plumber by trade. In November, 1892, he took the Bridgewater Arms Hotel, Gilbert-street, Runcorn, a fully licenseis house. The rent was £7O a year, off which the landl., d allowed him £2O a year. He paid nothing for goodwill but was chargid £2 17s. Od. per annum for the 11,13 of the fixtures. He bought the loose utensils fr-en the outgoing tenant at a valuation for about £l2. He had previously been manager of the Mariner's Hotel, Percival-lane, Runcorn. He added that Le La 4 no capital, but borrowed £3O frem his late wife, and £2O from friends. Bankrupt had not filed a defi- ciency aCC )unt, but says :—" Not having kept proper books of ac.lount, lam unable to explain my deficiency, except by stating that it has almost wholly arisen from the excess of my household and personal expenditure over my income." He alleged he only first became aware of his insolvency last November, and admitted tie had contracted debts since that time, which were still owing, hoping trade would revive. The unsecured li ..1 bilities were, except as to about £BO for money lent and interest, mainly trade liabilities. In part explanation of the fact that the bankrupt disclosed no assers, he said : " I live in furnished apartments now. I sold my gold watch and chain in January for £lB. and used the money to pay debts." In reply to Mr. Potter ,the bankrupt said that when he commenced business he owed about £25. He was in- solvent to that extent when he entered business, but he did not think that that was the cause of his present in- solvency, as £3O was his wife's. Bad trade commenced about November. There was a severe time of dopression from the frost. His business was entirely with boatmen. During the frost the boatmen were unable to follow their occupation. There was also a general staenation in trade in Roncorn. e did not think it necessary to keep a book of his accounts,and he had no record of his paa ments ex- cept the bills. He was first aware of his insolvency in November last, when his rent was due, and he was not able to pay it. About £3OO liablity had been incurred since he was aware of his insolvency. He kept on his business in the hop that trade would revive. He had been a member of the Runcorn District Council, and the election for that took place en Decem- ber 18th last year. Toe cost to him Wee £2 12s. He contested the election in the hope that it would be an inducement to increase his business. He thought that by serving on the Council, more people would come for refreshments to hi.t house. His exper- ience had however been that the result was otherwise, as there were certain people, who were also candidates who took exception to his being elected, and as far as possible prevented people from going to his house.—Mr. Potter : Is it a fact that some councillor said he would discharge any workman who entered your house P—l hive had it from the men, I have not hai,i it authentically. I do not want to place my- self suoject to libel; (continuing), the bankrupt , said that he had had family trouble, haym lost his wife. ,Ele obtained some beer from Greenall, Whitley, and Company on November 19th, representing that be had banked £42 owing. It was a habit of hie to write in the morning, and pay his accounts in the afternoon. It however slipped his memory to pay the money, and that was the reason that he had not paid the money. He had sufficient money in his safe at that time to pay the ' £42. He had paid this in various accoun.s slice. It was a complete oversight that he had not paid the above mentioned account. He paid £25 on account of the £42 to the traveller soon afterwards. Up to last Nov- ember, the house was paving him. TbB examination was adjourned until May 31st.

div.head: TEACHING IN SUNDAY SCHOOLS.
div.p: TEACHING IN SUNDAY SCHOOLS.
MEETING AF EARLESTOWN.

On Wednesday evening what was announced as a Sunday School mass meeting was held in the Wesleyan Chapel, Earlestown. The Rev. J. Bartley presided, and there were present with hilt] on the platform, the Revs. W. H. Parr, and S. Harper, of Liverpool, and Mr. P. Parr (secretary of the Sunday School). Tne Chairman said the object of the meeting was to increase the efficiency of the teaching, and to extend the interest of the congregation towards the sdhool, and he hoped there would be a marked increase of the pro- gress in the work accomplished by the Sunday School Mr. P. Parr said he would readout a few particulars which he had compiled to show the:reason why they de- sired agreaterinterest from their congregation and friends the Sunday School work. He thought the particulars would show that they were not making that progress which it was their desire to make, and as an outcome oh that meeting they trusted that their young men and women would specially take up the work with greater enthusiasm. The officers and teachers on the books were 14, number required each Sunday morning 34, after. noon 39 ; average attendance of teachers, morning 22, afternoon 32, thus showing that the average number oh teachers each Sunday morning was 12, . afternoon 7 Teachers meeting in Society 40 ; scholars on book-, select, 81; between 5 and 17 years old, 345 ; infants,44 total, 475. The average morning attendance was 154, aftern4on 280 ; average per class, morning 5, afternoon 9. They had a library containing 171 books, but it was at present closed owing to alterations. The scholars were taken to chapel regularly every Sunday morning. (Applause.) The Chairman said they had an average of 60s holars in the school every Sunday marning, without teachers, and in the afternoon 63 scholars without teachas, and that was a teaching staff of 76. .

The Rev. W. H. Parr, of Liverpool, said it was too late in the day to attempt a vindication of the Sunday school work of the past. Anyone who was old eneugh to remember the educational state of England 50 years ! ago, and compare it with that of to-day, would at once conclude that a vast advance had been made. Whilst some measure of the credit oi that advance was without doubt due to the increasing efficiency of their day school education, he claimed that the Sunday school claimed a fair proportion of the credit for thestateot affairs to day. He thought it was L vti Shaftesbury who said " if it was not for the Sunday schools, England would scarcely be a sate place to live in." Education had advaneed and children of to-day were not as the claildren of 50 years ago were. They were better educated, they knew a , great deal more ; it was no longer necessary to teach the ! alphabet in the Sunday school, and have a writing state there. Some people hastily jumped to the conclusion, that, admitting that there was need in the past, there was no longer the same need for Sunday school work to-day. His contention was that if there seas nee, 50 years ago, there was greater need today for Sabbath schools in England. It was a great mistake o suppose that scholarship meant saintliness. All the people who ; lived in villa residences with carriage drives sweeping round their lawn. were not good people, and all the hapless,luckless beings who dwelt in slum districts were not wicked people. Little children because they did not know much were not criminals; students, because they ! knew a great deal, were not the perfection of grsainess. Indeed scholarship might mean scoundrelism. Educate ; a man and they did not of necessity reform him ; they reformed the tools he worked with. They had Had some sorry exhibitions within the past few days that acesthe- ticism and literary abilities did not lift up the Christian education of man. For many years the Metho- dist people had insisted upon their minieers who stand in their pulpits being trained men, well equipped for their work ; it was none the less neeessary for teachers to be well cquipped for the ministry of the Sunday school in their classes. A Sunday school teacher had no right to shut his eyes to the work of preparation, and open his ,niouth to the work of teaching and see what God would send him. He recommended the putting ' on the shelves of the school library some good books that the teachers could use in the wora of preparation. ; They wanted at least half a dozen new teachers in the , school. He wondered if there was anyone present shal- low enough to think they were too good for Sunday school work,that it was not important enough for them,l or that they were just one step too high in refinement and social position to stoop to Sunday school work. If there were any such present he should say they were a great deal shallower than those who did " stoop " to Sunday school work. To-day they wanted the best mei' and best women. 'they could not over estimate the l importance of the work ; they must not shut their eyes to the fact that they were livingor should soon be living face to face with a time that might be perilous, with , questions that were of importance, and in a great measure as to how those questions were solved, and the ' spirit in which they were faced would depnnd upon the Sunday school of to-day. If they wanted social questions ; rightly solved, they must permeate them with religious teaching. A great Labour leader stated that in CIIPS^ days the church that only existed for spiritual functions ' had no right to exoit,and would cease to exist,that only in so far as the church competed in other organisations in the secular education of the people would it exist. He (the speaker) did not believe that. Religion was not dying ,sur, and it was not a waning force. He advised ' the teachers in their work to have patience with the children, they must not think that a restless boy was a vicious bsiy,or that a mischievous girl was a bad girl,t hey must not think that a child was a hopeless case because it was inattentive. They must bear with them, and endeavour to lead them aright. (Applause.) 'The P.ev. S. Harper also spoke on the same lines, and at the ciose,vetes of thanks were aecorc.eci the speakers.

div.head: CROWNING THE MAY QUEEN AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: CROWNING THE MAY QUEEN AT EARLESTOWN.

BRILLIANT SPECTACLE. Queen's weather favoured the fourth celebration of the tine honoured custom of crowning the May Queen at Eirlestown on Saturday afternoon, in fact a more brilliant clay for such an imposing affair as was witneseed could not well be imagined. From an early hbur, everybody was on the pai vice, and the preoara- tione for doing honour to tee festival were vigorously pushed forward, the humblest inhabitant vicing with those in the higher scale in their eagerness to excepting ethe iffAir a success. In the principal streets, perhaps Queen-street, where the residents appeared to be apathetic,there was a profuse display of bunting tines of streamers and flags being stretched across the streets from the upper windows of the houses and places a business. Soon after dinner the town began to wear an onnsually crowded appearance, reminding one of the Newton race days. To swell the gathering throngs large ()umbers of people from the outlying districts, especially Warrington, arrived by train at the Earlestown Station, whilst several warnnettes broueffs their quota of visitors from Haydock, Ashton, and Golborne, and long before the advertised time for the procession the line ot route was almost impassable. Extra policemen had been drafted into the town, ,nd these under the charge of Inseector Mcrgan, maintained order. The crowds were kept in good humour by witnessing the various eharamers, comic and otherwise, wending their way to the place of rencluzvous,a field near Vitriol-square. The time of assembly was put down at 1.45, and by this time the marshalling ground presented a lively appear- ance, the various costumes intermingline in kaleidos- copic faseion. The onerous duty of getting into some- thing like order such a heterogeneous Mass of huinan characters was then commenced, the task wheel fell to the lot of Messrs. G. Payne, J. Lowe, J. Gee and W. Renton. being at once a diffieult and unenviable one. The field was well adapted for the purpose, being spacious and convenient,but the task of finding Buffalo Bill, a Zulu Alley :eloper and such like characters to take their alotted pesiteena, from amongst such a varied crowd, was certainly not of the easiest kind, and by 230 the time annimused for making a start, the task seemed almost hopeless. Soon after three o'clock, how- ever,somethine like order was obtained, and prepere- tions made fer a start. The judges of the neatest and hest turnouts of horees.Stc , Messrs. Thorpe,thlbert,and Alderson had completed their task, and made their awards as follows :—Class 1. Ist prize, Sankey Sugar Company (carter, J. Dutton) ; 2nd, Messrs. J.Fairclough and Son (carter, .1. Claike) ; 3rd, J. Cawley. Class 2, Tradesmen, it, S. Bethel! (carter, G. Green), last year's first prize winner ; 2ed,E. L. Bent (cartier, .T. Lee) ; 3rd, Join Howe (carter, H. Hazeldine). A large number of vehicles and horses were placed at the disposal of the committee, the Midland Railway Company sending a couple of lurries from Warrington. The procession as stated, about three o'clock, moved off the field, headed by a vehicle containing the chairman of the committee. Rev. T R. Mathews, and the ladies committee, Mee- dames Valentine, Hazeton, and Ormand, who deserve the greatest praise for the interest and hard work they have infused into the festival, their duties in the matter 'of decoration and robing of the dancers, having been of the most exacting character. Following this convey- ance came another containing the smaller and young portion of a number of flower girls, whilst their elders followed on foot. Behind these came a juvenile repre- eentation of Robin Hood (Norman Pill) mounted on a p 'ay, and Maid Marion (Miss M. Taberner) a •companied by a band of Foresters in green. A tuither batch of flower girls was followed by a num- ber of juvenile marines drawing an eighty-one ton gun, outside which was a young marine, and following was a company of sailors. The Earlestown band here led up the fl ral, may pole, and rustic dancers, who were very prettily a'tired,and along the route, at intervals danced, something after the style of the Morris dancers, and the admiration of the onlookers was general. Farmers, Plouehmen and Rakers, preceded a conveyance with " no-peep," and Boy Blue (Master Walker), little Miss Muffi.'s, shepherds and sherherdesses, red riding hoods, colour boys, soldiers, hospital nurses, butchers, lady cricketers, and a handcart bedecked with branches of trees, amid which was a man made up in female attire, whilst pushing the cart, were several young fellows also in female attire, on the canopy being placed a placard with the inscription " Futcher Queen, 1 minute to late." Following this parody came a carriage containing " The Primrose Queen " (Miss Nield), attended by her train hearers (S. Maynes and H. Nield), and maids of honour (A. Kitchen, M. Siddeley, A. Walton, C. Booth, and F. Penketh). Then followed Mr. T. Molyneueslurry, con- taining a gigantic loaf, a yard or two long, joiners, artists, and painters, coopers and colliers. The Warring- ton Ragged School band brought up the next portion of the procession consisting of a lurry wit h glass bottle hands illustrating the process of glass-bottle making, bricksettere and labourers, clnggers, shae- makers, tailors, blacksmiths and strikers, dairymen and milkmaids, dressmakers, waitresses, gipsit s, flint glass hand,, with splendid specimens of their art, cricketers, fellowed by" Queen Rose Bud" (Miss M. Clarke), at- tended by her train hearers and maids of honour, Misses M. Peters, M Cs in., E. Evans, A. Vauselauke, N. Sheri- dan. E. Peters, M. Sheridan, S. A. Taylor, J. Busby, S. el. Lake, E. Evans, A. Dike, L. Sheridan A. Peters and A. Righy. Then came " The Prince," Sheridan, Hazleton, lion tamer. American chief, Buffalo Bill (E. Houghton) Mexican Joe (T. Watson), cowboys, jockeys, hunters, missing link, Zulu (R. Harrison), hunting girls, oil men and women, fruit girls, fairies„ Following these was a carriage and pair containing the ex-queen (Miss L.Chesters)in her robes of state,attended by her train bearers Masters Walton and Sutton. and maids of honour Misses H. Howarth, F. Rice, J. Massey, L. Heiman, A. Mnttram. Behind these came musicians. Italian girls and boys, Swiss girls and a comic group representing Ally Sloper (E. More- croft, wife (J. Watkinson) and family. Shylock,the Jew (R. 'Netkinson), American girls, sailor girls, lurry with Fairy Fay (Miss M. &Ahern) and attendant fairies,lurry with King of Imps (C. Rawlings) and attendants,repre- sentatives of Spring, Summer Autumn, and Winter, hosting, cricket, lawn tennis,and football. Foetbellers„ a Welshman with geateurry withßritannia (Miss Beston) surrounded les England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, I the British Army and Navy, and British Possessions, India, Anstralia,Canada,and Africa. Then came a motleyl group of clownierviggets,meshers,and as a set off a bevy of pretty flag drill eirls,charmingly attired. TheNutgrove band filled the next space, and they were followed by a Company of well drilled Highland soldiers, whose steady marching was favourably commented upon. & miniature policeman here kept the way for the Queen, who was preceded by the sword bearer (J. Marsh), sceptre bearer (W. Wetkinson), mimic archbishop bearing crown (F. Mullins). Bringing up tht rear wasthe Queen, (Miss M. E. Thompson,)in a carriage drawn by tour horses, with mitrides, and as guards of honour was a detachment of; the G Company lit V.B.S.L.R. P. W.V., under the com- mand of Sergeant Bailey. The Queen was attended by h.t pages (W. Smith and J. W. Appleton), train bearers (J Ogden and W.Gee),lady in waiting (Miss A Wadding- ton), maids pf honour (Misses M. Evans, M. A:Savage, B. Moulden, K. Taylor, B. Stokes, R. Day, M.A.Themas, and B. Caldwell). Altogether there were abut 2,000 children and others taking part in the procession, and the route taken was via Queen-st ,Fairclough-st ,Bridge. at., Mar ket-st„Legh-st., Sankey-et. Regent-et , Viaduct- t., Wood at., and Bank-at', to Earle Cottage, returning • by way of Eerle-st.and Market-st. to the grand-stand at Newton Common. We should say here that the "Prim- roee Queen" was crowned by Mrs. Brown, at her own home, in the presence of the neighbours, and was pre- sented with useful books. Co arrival at the grand-stand, each child was pre- sented with a bun and orange, and all order was at once an absent quantity. All the stands were crowded with spectators, lied it is expected that the affair will be a financial success. Some little time elapsed after the children had arrived within the enclosure before the subeequent proceedings commenced; the festivities in- cludina the introductionof the dancers. Then came the recenri,n of the various queens on the large platform, the May Queen ascending the throne erected at the end, after which she was presented with the seeptre,and then crowned "Queen of the May " by Mrs. Haxelton, wbo also presented her with a bible, and prayer-book, and hymn book. She was alsothe recipient of a cheque for £5 from Mr. S. Eiszelton, which was to be invested for ber until she reached the age of 21 years. The festivities before the Queen were afterwards pm. ceieled with, and consisted of a rustic dance, May-pole clanee,and floral dance,hympwards of 70 prettily dressed maidens. All the dances were executed under the super- intendence of Mr. George Slinn, whose labours in train- inger ptrh, be girlst th lay yi u been t pf the efficiency s most -witwith exacting hi which ar his- a ftheydridrill eptiapnielsapferr,,ln theoirine thousands d 'theirtasko, d the tors. applause f pect way also cleverly executed by a number of girls who had been trained by Mr. R. Jones, of Newton. A company and of hey.; attired as Highland soldiers also went through a drill and bayonet exercise in a very efficient manner, under the conductorship of Mr. Rimmer, who deserves great praise for the remarkable pitch of efficiency to which he had brought the boys, when it is considered that he had only three weeks at his disposal in which to train them. At the close of the dancing, Ste, the Rev. P. R. Matthews expressed thanks on behalf of the committee to all those wire had assisted in the success of thee festival. C meiderine the dimensions of the undertaking.. the varicus arreneements were fairly well carried out by a cominitteieincludine the ladies' committee already men- tioned,and also consieting of Messrs. W.Banton,J.Lewe, S.Openshaw, W Baston, J. Gee.J.Burrows.ll Crowther, G. Payne, C. Ilamblett, G. Butler, I. Clarke, %V. Lan- warm.. J. Turten, J. Bercroft ; financial sectary, Mr. T. Latimer ; secretary, Mr. J. Waddington, upon whom, a good share of the work, of course fell ; and treasurer.' Mr. T. Mnlyneux, The Eirlestown band played for , dancing until dusk. The town until late into the nigh! presented a very busy appearance,the Market place being ' ,urned into a gigantic fair, the purveyors of hobby horses, sheeting galleries, At., doing an excellent busi- ness.

div.head: EXHIBITION OF BILLIARDS AT 1 RUNCORN.
div.p: EXHIBITION OF BILLIARDS AT 1 RUNCORN.
DAWSON v. DIGGLE.

- - - At Runcorn Liberal Club, on Wed, esday, a grand ex- hibition game 01 billiards between C. Dawson and E. Diggle, two of the best billiard players in the North of England, was witnessed. Two games-of 1,000 up were played, one in the afternoon and the other at night. The contests took place in the billiard room of the Out), and in order to accommodate the spec, ators special prepara- tions had been made. The billiard tables with the ex- ception of the one which was used, were taken out of the room and platforms were erected. Pruin these a good view of the game was obtained. There was a good attendance both afternoon and evening. Play was be- gun promptly on time, and Diggle soon began to assert supremacy by a fair lead. A good break of 64 was male by Dawson when his score stood at 158 as against 308. Diggle followed with a break of 24 and a later with one 6,1 85. This brou.lht his total up to 432, whilst his opponents stood at 203. DIWEOR was m-ire suc- cessful in his next essay, scoring 43. Diggle replied with one ot 23, but Dawson by a fine piece of play made a break of 98 bringing the totals a little nearer equal, viz. 344 as against 450 by Diggle. This, however, was Dawson's most noteworthy score during the afternoon, for from this time to the close of the g.. me Diggle lead the way,scoring at a rate rapid whilst his 'pp-merit lagged woefully behind. Diggle's scores included one break of 85, another of 248, and a little later he struck the 1000 with a brilliantly unfinished break of 169. The scores at the conclusion of the game were Diggle 1000, Dawson 377. The game lasted two hours, and Diggle's fine display, more particularly in "nursery cannons„" was a treat to witness. Play was resnmed ateight o'clock. Dawson commenced splendidly, snaking two breaks ot 31 and 71 respectively,while his opponent's largest score was 16. Dawson continued to laid. and In a short time aided he two breaks of 30 and 70 he brought his tail up to 347. Diggle's score had not yet reached three figures, it standing at 99. He, however, compiled 48 in his next essay which Dawson responded to with a break of 58. Matters still went badly with Wggle for Dawson gained the respectable lead of 438 to 155. In his next attempt Uggle was more successful, scoring 100, and shortly afterwards he drew near his opponent's total with breaks of 87 and 65. Dawson played pluckily to maintai•3 his lead, his next best break being one of 46 • He gradually worked his score up to 599, but his opponent aided by a break of 55 had reached we 500's, and at one bound with a splendid break of 115 he passed him amidst the applause of the spectators. By good play Dawson eventually secured the lead again, the score being : Dawson, 706 ; Diggle, 694. A neck and neck struggle ensued for the next few mance Ayres until Diggle by a break of 143 placed himself in a decided advance. With the score standing at 908 Diggle, 755 Dawson; the chances of the latter cueist ked ominous. But in his next attempt he compiled 82 ; Diggle only followed with 12. Dawson put on another 35 whicil Diggle responded to with 19 bringing up his score to 939 as against 872. Now came the surprise of the evening for Dawson in his next essay, concluded the match by scoring his necessary 128 to complete the 1,000. It is a matter of course to say that the effort received the warmest plaudits of the audience. The arrangements or the nritch were successfully carried ont by a small committee consisting of Messrs. R.Moore, W. Wright, Brimelow and Halliday.

div.head: RUNCORN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL
div.p: RUNCORN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL
UN lON.

The Rev. Thomas Brackenbury presided at the annual meeting of this union held in Brunswick vestry on Friday evening. Representatives were present from the Wesleyan Sunday schools in connection with Brunswick, Mill Brow, Camden, Nelson-street, Weston and Halton., The number of schools in the union numbers 8; teachers , and officers, 208; scholars, 2,074. The visitors report for the year was read by Mr. J. D. Jones. It stated that it was gratifying to find that the schools showed no fall- ing off in numbers. This large attendance of children brought with it a great responsibility which could not be lightly esteemed. There were two considerations which intensified this responsibility more than was generally noticed. The Education Act of 1870 had been at work for 25 years, and the influence it had exerted must be incalculable. No one woull eeny that as a result of the working of that Act religious instruction, as Sunday school teachers undertood the term, had almost dis- appeared. No blame need be cast upon the teachers in National Schools, because they did not make so much of the spiritual tfaining of the children as the teachers of a former generation. Elementary teachers were appointed now because of their ability to teach the three lt.'s, and a rigid examination had to be passed before their efficiency was certified. It was no wonder, then, that the spiritual atmosphere that formerly pervaded the schoolroom had given place to hard grinding at secular studies. Practically speaking, the teacher was a Gov- ernment official, and to make him a preacher would be a mistake; indeed to attempt it would be seeking to accomplish theimpossible task of "making men moral by Act of Parliament.' The result of this changed condition of things was that the work of cultivating the spiritual nature of the ckild was relegated to 'one day out of the seven and where the parents did not feel it their duty to take this work in hand it had to be dene by the Sunday school teacher. This added responsibility became too much at times for the conscientious teacher to bear, and if he relied on his own ability to do the work devolving upon him he would break. down. The second consideration that increased the responsibility of the modern Sunday school teacher else arose out of the working of the Education Act. The superior methods of training in the day school during the week which now obtained, produced smarter and more intelligent children than in the " good old days and as they did not believe in the old sneer that • ignor- ance is the mother of devotion," it was only reasonable to expect that the intelligence of the week day would ' call for its counterpart on the Sung:late. Boys and girls accustomed to the treatment of history, grammar, geo- graphy, arithmetic and even physical scienc.at the hands of skilful and, highly trained teachers expected a treatment not less skilful of Bible narratives and Chris- tian doctrines in the Sunday school. Hence came the pressure of work,and the conscientious teacher excl rimed " who is sufficient for these things ? "It was something for which to be thankful that although the work was so exacting the Runcorn circuit commanded the services of so large a band of devoted toilers in this interesting field of labour. Judging from the teachers ass whole they appeared to be fairly efficient. Of course when it was considered that the whole of the work was voluntary it would he too much to expect to find perfection in the teaching staff of any school ; but it would be readily conceded that between our present condition and per- fection there was a vast difference. What was the ob- ject the average teacher pliced before himself when taking up the work ? It was the teacher's ideal that de- termined the amount and the character of his work. If a teacher took no trouble over his class, were thee to judge that he only expected a crop of weeds ? The work called loudly for the conservation of the highest culture and the deepest devotion the church possessed. The order in the schools generally was very good, and showed that the superintendents had their schools under control, a very essential element in successful Sunday school work. Seine of the school premises seemed rather unsuitable for the purpose of effieient teaching. More classroom accommodation was one consideration. The vexed question of ventilation was still an unsolved pro- blem. Most of the schools would be the bet ter fora perio- dical acquaintance with the whitewash brush. The musical portion of the school work was very good throughout the circuit; each school - possessing either harmonium or piano to lead the singing; though at one school visited the accompanist did not turn up until after the singing of the first hymn, which had a disas trous effect upon the opening exercises. At one school the Lord's prayer was very sweetly chanted by the whole school. This seemed an innovation, and coming as it did witheut any warning might have been expected to produce a feeling of irritation, but the reverse was the case. While on the question of singing it had occurred to thee, that it would conduce to the maintenance of order at the close of the school if a hymn were sung as the scholars leave the school. The work in connection with the various Bands of Hope had been carried with success during the season; and in the schools, where libraries were still in existence a very good aacount was given of the use the children m tele of the literature pro- vided them. Why the establishment of a free library in the town shonld have been looked upon as a reason for Closing the Sunday school libraries was a puzzle to one of the visitors. Methodist literature pro- vides a rich storehouse, where the special wants of the young 'Methodist could besupplied, and every Methodist Sunday school should have a distinctive Methodist library at the service of thechildren of their people. Such an Institution would do away With the lamentable lack of knowledge on the history of Methodism which pre- vailed and which was accountable for the many defec- tions from the Church of those who owed her so much, yeung man saturated with the traditions and history of Wesleyan Methodism contained in its literature would lightly throw off the ties which bound him to the Church of his childhood.

A hearty and unanimous vote of thanks was passed to the visitors (Messrs. J. M. Fri and J. D. Jones) for their services during the year. Messrs. James toolter , (Halton) and J. Leech, jun. (Brunswick), were appointed visitors for the ensuing year. A well-deserved vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Walter Millington for so ably fulfilling the duties of secretary. As he was unable to continue in the office, Mr. Arthur Dutton (Camden) was elected.

div.p: UPPER MERSEY WATERMEN AND THE
SHIP CANAL.

div.head: DEPUTATION TO MR. COLLIER. '
div.p: DEPUTATION TO MR. COLLIER. '

On Saturday evening a well-attended meeting of members of the Upper Mersey Watermen and Porters' Association was held in the Union Hall, Runcorn, to consider their future attitude towards the Manchester Ship Canal Company Bridgewater ; Undertaking. The principal topic under dinus- sion was what the waterinen contend is a breach of the agreement entered into between them and the company at the beginning of last year, and es- pecially with regard to Sunday travelling and dock rates. There are also several minor matters rt.quiri rig adjustment. '1 hose present, after discuss- ing the subject, expressed their determination to have the agreement carried out in its entirety; and unless this was done, the matter of coming out on strike would be taken seriously into considera- tion. •

On Tuesday the representatives of the Upper Mersey Watermen and Porters' Association held an interview with Mr. Collier, of the Bridgewater Undertaking, Manchester. on Tuesday, for the pur- pose of considering what the Association contend is a breach of the agreement which was arrived at early in 1894. A number of points were discussed and as there was a difference of opinion regarding several clauses,Mr Collier expressed his willingness for the matter to be referred to arbitration. A num- ber of names will be submitted, and one will be selected to represent the Watermen's Association.

A concert was held on Friday evening week in connection with the Church Lads' Brigade, in the schoolroom After a miscellaneous pro- gramme, the members of the Brigade Ambulance Class, who have been under the tuition of P.S. Barnes,appeared;in the characters of ambulance men dressing and attending to the wounded. During an interval in the programme the Rev. J. J. Lang- ham,chaplain to the brigade, referred to the credit- able performance of the Ambulance Class, which,he said, reflected the greatest credit upon their excel- lent instructor, Sergeant Barnes. (Applause.) Mr. Langham then presented to Sergeant. Barnes a silver pencil as a memento of his services to the class. Sergeant Barnes suitably acknowledged the gift. On Tuesday evening, Father Firth met Mr. Dunne with a view to deciding the right of entering the final stage of this competition. Four games had previously been played of which each player had won one, the other two being drawn. Father Firth had the move and Mr. Dunne adopted the French defence ; a very close gagne ensued resulting in the victory of the former. Fatter Firth will now have to meet either Canon Dodd or Mr. Chandler between , whom matters are still unsettled, they having played two games, one en4ing in a draw and the other being placed to the credit of Mr. Chandler. It should be explained that the competition is being fought on the knockout principle by the scoring of the first two wins, draws being disregarded. L&WN °WHYS. •GARLAND , Ironmonger. div.head: _ DROWNING FATALITY AT GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: _ DROWNING FATALITY AT GRAPPENHALL.

Mr. H. C. Yates held an inquest on Monday, at the Dog and Dart Inn, Grappenhall, on the body of Ralph Harrison, aged two years and nine months, who was drowned in the Bridgewater Canal, on Friday afternoon.—Rannah Harrison, mother of the deceased, said that her husband, James Harrison, and herself lived at Astlev Green, near Manchester. tie was a flat man. On Friday she and deceased were alone on hoard the flat Wright, which was tied near to Mr. Lomas's coal wharf, Cliff-lane, Grappenhall. Her husband was away at the time at Northwich. The little lad was in the batches. She went to move HOLES planks, telling deceased to stay whore he was. She was sway about ten minutes,and on returning she missed him. She then gave the alarm.—Mr. Fairhurst said that about four o'clock on Friday be heard screams, and went to see what was the matter. Seeing a body in the water, he got. a boathook and pulled it out of the water from toe stern end of the boat. The child was then dead, having been in the water about three-quarters of an hour.—The jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dentally drowned." Thh Onurch Missionary Society annual sermons were held in Sunday in St. Peter's Chnrch,at which place the pulpit was occupied in the morning by thh Right Rev. Bishop Royston, who took for his text St. Matthew xxviii. 18, 19, 20. The Bishop pointed out how glad he was to find that this church I had taken up such an important work as the mis- sion work, and he believed that this was the second year they had supported that cause. There were over 40 churches that day in which anniversary sermons were being deliveaed. He alluded to what was being done in various parts of the mission field, especially in Uganda, and pointed out what a won- derful change had iaken place in that country dur- ing the past few years. In the evening a sermon was delivered by the Rev. B. Percival, vicar of St. Peter's, which also was of an interesting nature. There were large congregations, and collections were made in aid of the Church fklinsionary Society. —Other services on behalf of the society were held on Sunday morning, afternoon and evening in St. Ann's Church, The pulpit at the evening service was occupied by Bishop Royston who delivered a suitable address on the operations of the society.

THE CHARGES AGAINST SABEZ BALFOUR. The hearing of the charges against Jabez Spencer Bal- four was resumed at Bow-street on Monday. Evidence was given by Mr. L. B. Burns, the prisoner's nephew,and by Mr. T. Golding, a member of the firm of solicitors who had acted for the company called " Whitehall Court, Limited," with reference to certain transactions between that Company and the House and Land Invest- ment Trust. The case was again adjourned. • The preamble ef a bill enabling the Mersey Railway Company to use electricity as a motive power was on Monday passed by a Committee of the House of Lords, presided over by Lord Harris. A workmen's train and a ballast train collided on Mon- day morning on a portion of the London and North- Western Rail way now being constructed near Southern, Leamington. A portion of the workmen's train was telescoped. o,w man was killed and eighteen were in- ured, five being detained in hospital.
